how: Every vector can be split along three perpendicular axes, so it is fully fixed by three numbers (its components). Adding vectors means adding these numbers, and scaling means multiplying each of them by the scalar.
Collinearity needs only that the direction is the same line. If two vectors point along one line, one is a scalar multiple of the other, so their component ratios are equal.
The multiple may be negative, which is why a and -a are collinear even though they point opposite ways.
cases: Parallel to the same line is the exact condition for collinear vectors; the vectors need not be equal in size or sense.
Vectors a and -a: collinear (anti-parallel), equal magnitude, sum is the null vector.
Zero vector is parallel to every vector and its magnitude is 0.
Coplanar vectors: lie in or parallel to one plane. Collinear vectors are always coplanar.
Like vectors point the same way; unlike vectors point opposite ways.
Direction of a vector in the answer must always be stated; a bare number is a scalar.
Acceleration, force, velocity, displacement, momentum are vectors; speed, distance, mass, energy, work, power, pressure, current are scalars.
values: i, j, k are unit vectors along x, y, z axes with |i| = |j| = |k| = 1.
Unit of acceleration is m/s^2 and it is a vector; speed also has m/s but is a scalar.
Unit vector along a = a/|a|; for example along 3i - 4j it is (3i - 4j)/5 since |a| = 5.
Common magnitudes: |i + j| = sqrt2, |i + j + k| = sqrt3, |i + 2j + 2k| = 3.
uses: Resolving forces, velocities and displacements in mechanics and navigation.
Checking whether three points lie on a straight line (surveying, runway alignment).
Finding unit vectors for directions such as wind or heading.
mistakes: Calling a quantity with a unit like m/s^2 a scalar; direction decides, not the unit alone.
Thinking collinear vectors must have the same direction; opposite direction is also collinear.
Computing PQ as tail minus head instead of head minus tail.
Forgetting that a unit vector must be divided by the magnitude, not just by the largest component.
exam: AAI style: one-line theory questions such as which quantity is a vector or what makes vectors collinear. Practice: Unit vector along 3i - 4j? [(3i - 4j)/5] Are 2i + 4j and -i - 2j collinear? [Yes, a = -2b] Magnitude of i + 2j + 2k? [3]
Which is a vector: speed, work, force? [force]

topics.title: Dot (Scalar) Product and Its Applications
overview: The dot product of two vectors gives a scalar. It measures how much one vector points along the other. It is the main tool in the chapter for finding angles, testing perpendicularity, projections and for expanding squares of sums of vectors.

In AAI JE papers dot product questions are usually short: compute a.b from components, find an unknown constant for perpendicular vectors, find an angle in a triangle, or use the identity for |a+b+c|^2.

terms.meaning: a.b = |a||b|cos(theta), where theta (0 to pi) is the angle between the vectors placed tail to tail.
Vectors with a.b = 0 (non-zero vectors at 90 degrees).
Scalar (a.b)/|b|; the vector projection is ((a.b)/|b|^2) b.
Angle at a vertex of a triangle uses the two vectors leaving that vertex.

formulas: Component form: a.b = a1 b1 + a2 b2 + a3 b3.
Angle: cos(theta) = (a.b)/(|a||b|).
Commutative: a.b = b.a. Distributive: a.(b + c) = a.b + a.c.
i.i = j.j = k.k = 1 and i.j = j.k = k.i = 0.
Perpendicular test: a.b = 0 for non-zero a, b.
Cauchy-Schwarz: |a.b| is less than or equal to |a||b|.
Angle at B of triangle ABC: cos(B) = (BA.BC)/(|BA||BC|).
Angle between a and b is acute for a.b positive, right for zero, obtuse for negative.
a.a = |a|^2, so |a| = sqrt(a.a); a.b is a scalar and and a.b = |a| times the scalar projection of b on a.
how: From a.b = |a||b|cos(theta), the product is large and positive when the vectors point the same way, zero at 90 degrees, and negative when they point apart.
In components the cross terms like i.j vanish because the axes are perpendicular, leaving a1 b1 + a2 b2 + a3 b3.
Expanding (a + b).(a - b) uses distributivity: a.a - a.b + b.a - b.b. Since a.b = b.a the middle terms cancel, giving |a|^2 - |b|^2.
Squaring a sum of three vectors in the same way produces the three squares plus twice every pair product; if the sum is zero, the pair-sum equals minus half of the sum of squares.
cases: theta = 0: a.b = |a||b| (maximum). theta = 180 degrees: a.b = -|a||b| (minimum).
theta = 90 degrees: a.b = 0; this is how an unknown constant is found for perpendicular vectors.
Acute angle if a.b is positive, obtuse if a.b is negative.
If |a + b| = |a - b| then a and b are perpendicular.
a.b = 0 does not force a or b to be zero; one may be the zero vector or they may be perpendicular.
Dot product is not associative: (a.b).c has no meaning because a.b is a scalar.
values: i.i = j.j = k.k = 1 and all mixed products i.j, j.k, k.i are 0.
uses: Work done W = F.d (force dot displacement).
Finding angles between edges, cables or runways given coordinates.
Component (projection) of a force along a direction.
mistakes: Using the angle at the wrong vertex; for angle ABC use BA and BC, not AB and BC.
Forgetting that cos(theta) = (a.b)/(|a||b|) needs both magnitudes; leaving a root out of the denominator.
Sign slip in the perpendicular condition, giving wrong constants; expand carefully and set the total to zero.
Writing a.b as a vector or giving it a direction.
exam: AAI style: compute a.b, find the constant for perpendicular vectors, or use the squared-sum identity. Practice: a = i + 2j + 3k, b = 4i - j + k: a.b? [5] Perpendicular if 2i + j and i + p j? [p = -2] |a| = 3, |b| = 4, a perpendicular b: |a + b|? [5]

topics.title: Cross (Vector) Product and Unit Normals
overview: The cross product of two vectors is a new vector perpendicular to both. Its magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram on the two vectors. It is used to find normals to planes, areas, moments (torque) and to test for parallel vectors.
Together with the dot product, the cross product is the second main operation in the chapter, and the AAI paper often mixes the two.

terms.meaning: a x b = |a||b| sin(theta) n_hat, where n_hat is the unit vector given by the right hand rule.
Curl fingers from a to b; the thumb gives the direction of a x b.
|a x b|; area of triangle with sides a and b is half of |a x b|.
Unit vector perpendicular to a plane: +-(a x b)/|a x b|.
Result of a x b when a and b are parallel or one is zero.

formulas: a x b = |a||b| sin(theta) n_hat and |a x b| = |a||b| sin(theta).
Determinant form: a x b = det of rows (i j k), (a1 a2 a3), (b1 b2 b3) = (a2 b3 - a3 b2) i - (a1 b3 - a3 b1) j + (a1 b2 - a2 b1) k.
Anti-commutative: b x a = -(a x b).
Distributive: a x (b + c) = a x b + a x c.
i x j = k, j x k = i, k x i = j; reversing the order gives minus sign; i x i = j x j = k x k = 0.
a x a = 0, and a x b = 0 means a and b are parallel (if non-zero).
Area of triangle ABC = (1/2)|AB x AC|; area of parallelogram = |a x b|.
Lagrange identity: |a x b|^2 + (a.b)^2 = |a|^2 |b|^2.
Triple product: a x (b x c) = (a.c) b - (a.b) c.
Scalar triple product [a b c] = a.(b x c) = determinant of the three rows of components; |[a b c]| is the volume of the parallelepiped.
Vectors a, b, c are coplanar if [a b c] = 0. Volume of tetrahedron = |[a b c]|/6.
how: The magnitude |a||b| sin(theta) is the base times the height of the parallelogram, hence the area.
The direction must be perpendicular to both vectors, so it is along the normal of the plane that contains a and b; the right hand rule picks one of the two possible normals.
Because the result depends on the order of operands, swapping them reverses the direction. For unit vectors, i x j = k follows the cyclic order i, j, k; going against the cycle gives a minus sign.
The triple product expansion a x (b x c) = (a.c) b - (a.b) c shows that the result lies in the plane of b and c.
cases: theta = 0 or 180 degrees: a x b = 0 (parallel). theta = 90 degrees: |a x b| = |a||b| (maximum).
Exactly two unit vectors are perpendicular to the plane of two non-parallel vectors, namely +(a x b)/|a x b| and -(a x b)/|a x b|.
If a and b are parallel there are infinitely many perpendicular unit vectors, since a x b = 0 gives no direction.
i x (j x k) = i x i = 0, j x (k x i) = j x j = 0, k x (i x j) = k x k = 0, so their sum is the null vector.
|a x b| = |a.b| means tan(theta) = 1 so theta = 45 degrees (or 135 degrees if obtuse is allowed).
a x b is perpendicular to both a and b, so (a x b).a = 0 and (a x b).b = 0.
Cross product is not associative: a x (b x c) is not equal to (a x b) x c in general.
values: sin0 = 0, sin30 = 1/2, sin45 = 1/sqrt2, sin60 = sqrt3/2, sin90 = 1.
j x i = -k, k x j = -i, i x k = -j (reverse cyclic order gives minus).
uses: Torque = r x F and angular momentum = r x p in physics.
Area of a triangular plot or face from vertex coordinates.
Finding normal vectors to planes for 3D geometry.
mistakes: Writing the determinant with the wrong sign on the middle (j) term.
Giving only one unit normal; there are always two (plus and minus).
Treating a x b as commutative.
Forgetting that a x b is a vector while a.b is a scalar, so a x (b x c) and (a x b).c are very different.
exam: AAI style: count or find unit vectors perpendicular to a plane, simplify triple products of i, j, k, or use magnitude relations. Practice: i x j + j x k + k x i? [i + j + k] Area of parallelogram on i + j and j + k? [sqrt3]
Unit vector perpendicular to i and j? [+-k] sin(theta) = cos(theta) angle? [45 degrees]

topics.title: Resultant of Velocities and Parallelogram Law
overview: When a body or point has several velocities at once, they combine by vector addition into a single resultant velocity. The parallelogram law gives the resultant of two, and the component method gives the resultant of any number.
This is the application side of vector addition and appears in questions on navigation, wind and aircraft ground speed, and fill in the blank theory questions.

terms.meaning: Single vector equivalent to the combined effect of several vectors.
If two vectors from a point are the adjacent sides of a parallelogram, their resultant is the diagonal from that same point.
Resolve each vector along x and y, add components separately, then recombine.
Place vectors head to tail; the closing side from first tail to last head is the resultant.
Resultant is zero (closed polygon).

formulas: Two vectors P and Q at angle theta: R = sqrt(P^2 + Q^2 + 2 P Q cos(theta)).
Direction of R from P: tan(alpha) = Q sin(theta)/(P + Q cos(theta)).
For many vectors V_i at angles theta_i from a reference: Rx = sum of V_i cos(theta_i), Ry = sum of V_i sin(theta_i).
R = sqrt(Rx^2 + Ry^2) and angle = arctan(Ry/Rx) (check the quadrant from the signs of Rx, Ry).
If angles are given between consecutive vectors, add them up to get each angle from the first vector.
Perpendicular vectors: R = sqrt(P^2 + Q^2), tan(alpha) = Q/P.
Equal magnitudes P at angle theta: R = 2P cos(theta/2).
Relative velocity of A with respect to B: v_AB = v_A - v_B.
Difference of two vectors: |P - Q| = sqrt(P^2 + Q^2 - 2 P Q cos(theta)), theta being the angle between them tail to tail.
Lami theorem: for three forces in equilibrium, each force over the sine of the angle between the other two is the same.
how: Draw the parallelogram on two vectors with the same starting point. The diagonal through that point has x and y parts equal to the sums of the parts of the two sides, which is exactly vector addition.
Applying cosine rule to the triangle formed gives R^2 = P^2 + Q^2 + 2PQ cos(theta), since the interior angle is 180 degrees minus theta.
For several vectors the component method is safest: each vector contributes V cos(angle) to x and V sin(angle) to y, and the sum of components of the sum equals the sum of components.
Always convert decimal degrees to minutes by multiplying the decimal part by 60.
cases: theta = 0: R = P + Q (maximum). theta = 180 degrees: R = |P - Q| (minimum).
Three or more vectors forming a closed polygon have resultant zero.
Fill in the blank law: velocities represented by two sides of a parallelogram from a point are equivalent to a single velocity represented by the diagonal from the same point.
A 'given angle between consecutive vectors' problem needs cumulative angles (30, then 30 + 90 = 120, then 120 + 120 = 240).
If Rx is negative and Ry positive the resultant lies in the second quadrant; add 180 degrees to the principal arctan value.
Decimal 24.9 degrees = 24 degrees 54 minutes because 0.9 x 60 = 54.
values: 1 degree = 60 minutes, so 0.9 degree = 54 minutes.
uses: Aircraft heading plus wind gives ground track and ground speed.
River crossing and boat problems.
Net force on a structure from several cables.
mistakes: Using the angle between consecutive vectors directly as the angle from the reference direction.
Taking the diagonal formula with minus instead of plus when the angle is measured tail to tail.
Ignoring the quadrant when finding the angle by arctan.
Mixing degree-minute and decimal degree forms.
exam: AAI style: a numerical multi-velocity problem with option pairs of speed and angle, or the sides and diagonal fill in the blank. Practice: 3 and 4 at 90 degrees, R? [5] Two equal velocities of 10 at 120 degrees, R? [10] 6 and 8 at 0 degrees, R? [14]
6 and 8 at 180 degrees, R? [2]

topics.title: 3D Coordinates, Distance and Section Formula
overview: Three dimensional geometry starts with a point fixed by three coordinates (x, y, z) measured from the origin along three perpendicular axes. The coordinate planes divide space into eight octants.
This topic covers where points lie, distance between points, and the section formula for dividing a segment internally or externally. It is the foundation for lines and planes.

terms.meaning: XY-plane (z = 0), YZ-plane (x = 0), ZX-plane (y = 0).
One of the 8 regions formed by the three planes, fixed by signs of x, y, z.
Point lies between P1 and P2 and splits the segment in ratio m:n.
Point lies on the extended line outside the segment, with distances in ratio m:n.
Point dividing the segment in ratio 1:1.

formulas: Distance: PQ = sqrt((x2-x1)^2 + (y2-y1)^2 + (z2-z1)^2).
Distance of P(x,y,z) from origin: sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2).
Internal division in m:n: ((m x2 + n x1)/(m+n), (m y2 + n y1)/(m+n), (m z2 + n z1)/(m+n)).
External division in m:n: ((m x2 - n x1)/(m-n), (m y2 - n y1)/(m-n), (m z2 - n z1)/(m-n)).
Centroid of triangle: average of the three vertices; centroid of tetrahedron: average of four vertices.
Parametric form of a point on segment AB: A + t(B - A), with 0 less than or equal to t less than or equal to 1.
Collinearity of A, B, C: AB + BC = AC in length or direction ratios of AB and BC proportional.
Distance of P(x,y,z) from x-axis = sqrt(y^2 + z^2); from y-axis = sqrt(x^2 + z^2); from z-axis = sqrt(x^2 + y^2).
Distance of P(x,y,z) from the XY-plane = |z|; from the YZ-plane = |x|; from the ZX-plane = |y|.
Reflection of (x,y,z) in the XY-plane is (x,y,-z); in the YZ-plane (-x,y,z); in the ZX-plane (x,-y,z); in the origin (-x,-y,-z).
how: The point dividing P1P2 internally in ratio m:n is a weighted average of the end points with weights n for P1 and m for P2.
For external division the point lies beyond P2 (if m is larger than n), so one distance is longer and the weights have opposite signs, which is why the formula uses m - n in the denominator.

The parametric form A + t(B - A) is the same section formula with t = m/(m+n). A point lies on the segment only if t is between 0 and 1. If one coordinate is the same at both ends, it stays the same along the whole segment.
cases: Point (a, b, 0) lies on the XY-plane; (0, b, c) on the YZ-plane; (a, 0, c) on the ZX-plane.
Point on x-axis: (a, 0, 0); on y-axis: (0, b, 0); on z-axis: (0, 0, c).
Ratio m:n with m equal to n has no external point (the denominator is zero); the point goes to infinity.
Ratio is external when the answer lies outside the segment; using a negative ratio in the internal formula gives the external division point.
Coordinate that is equal at both end points is unchanged in every point of the segment (for example y = 2 at both ends gives y = 2).
Signs of (x, y, z) fix the octant: (+,+,+) is the first octant.
Distance formula is symmetric: PQ = QP.
values: Octant signs: (+,+,+) first; (-,+,+) second; (-,-,+) third; (+,-,+) fourth; the lower four have z negative.
Midpoint has ratio 1:1 and the centroid of a triangle divides each median 2:1 from the vertex.
uses: Locating points and plotting positions in 3D space.
Finding midpoint, centroid, or a point a given fraction along a path.
Checking if points lie on a line or plane in surveying and design.
mistakes: Using the internal formula for an external ratio (or the plus sign instead of minus).
Swapping the points: m goes with the second point P2, n with the first.
Confusing the XY-plane (z = 0) with the z-axis (x = y = 0).
Forgetting to divide by m + n or m - n.
exam: AAI style: ask the plane or axis on which a point lies, or one coordinate of a dividing point. Practice: midpoint of (2,4,6) and (4,2,0)? [(3,3,3)] Distance from origin to (2,3,6)? [7] Internal 1:2 point of (0,0,0) and (3,3,3)? [(1,1,1)]
Point on segment (1,1,1) to (3,5,7) with x = 2? [(2,3,4)]

topics.title: Direction Cosines and Direction Ratios
overview: A line in space has a direction. Direction cosines (dc's) are the cosines of the angles the line makes with the positive x, y and z axes. Direction ratios (dr's) are any three numbers proportional to the direction cosines.
They are the main data used to describe lines, to find angles between lines and to test parallel or perpendicular lines.

terms.meaning: l = cos(alpha), m = cos(beta), n = cos(gamma) for angles alpha, beta, gamma with the positive axes.
Numbers a, b, c proportional to l, m, n.
The direction ratios of vector a1 i + a2 j + a3 k are its components (a1, a2, a3).
Direction cosines of the opposite direction are (-l, -m, -n).
Fixed values for x, y, z axes.

formulas: l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1 (and cos^2(alpha) + cos^2(beta) + cos^2(gamma) = 1).
From ratios (a, b, c): l = a/sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2), m = b/sqrt(...), n = c/sqrt(...).
Line through P(x1,y1,z1) and Q(x2,y2,z2): dr's are (x2-x1, y2-y1, z2-z1).
Equal ratio form: dc's are proportional to dr's, so a/l = b/m = c/n = sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2).
sin^2(alpha) + sin^2(beta) + sin^2(gamma) = 2.
Line with equal angles to all axes: l = m = n = +-1/sqrt3.
Two lines parallel: dr's proportional. Two lines perpendicular: a1 a2 + b1 b2 + c1 c2 = 0.
Direction cosines of a vector are the components of its unit vector.
Angle between two lines with direction cosines (l1,m1,n1) and (l2,m2,n2): cos(theta) = l1 l2 + m1 m2 + n1 n2.
Projection of a segment of length d on the x, y, z axes are d l, d m, d n.
how: A unit vector along a line has components equal to the cosines of its angles with the axes, because the projection of a unit vector on an axis is cos(angle).
Since a unit vector has length 1, squares of the components add to 1; this is l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1.

Direction ratios are not unique: multiplying all by a non-zero number gives another valid set. To get the cosines, divide by the length so the sum of squares becomes 1. A line has two sets of dc's, one for each sense, differing in sign.
cases: Equal angle with all axes: cos^2(alpha) = 1/3 so dc's are (1/sqrt3, 1/sqrt3, 1/sqrt3), with the minus set also possible when the angles are not all acute.
Angles 60, 135, 120 degrees: cosines 1/2, -1/sqrt2, -1/2; check 1/4 + 1/2 + 1/4 = 1.
Any set of three angles must satisfy the square-sum condition; not all angle triples are possible.
A line in the XY-plane has n = 0.
A line parallel to an axis has the other two dc's equal to 0.
Dc's of the line through the origin and (a, b, c) are a, b, c divided by the distance.
values: Axes: x (1,0,0), y (0,1,0), z (0,0,1). Equal angles with axes: +-(1/sqrt3, 1/sqrt3, 1/sqrt3), each angle about 54.74 degrees.
uses: Describing the heading of a line, cable or flight path in 3D.
Computing the angle between two lines or between a line and a plane.
Finding the equation of lines using the direction ratios.
mistakes: Writing the angle value as the dc; the dc is the cosine of the angle.
Forgetting the negative cosine for obtuse angles such as 135 degrees and 120 degrees.
Saying the dc's of a line are unique; direction reversal changes all signs.
Not normalising ratios before using l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1.
exam: AAI style: give angles and ask the cosines, or ask the dc's of the axes or of a line with equal angles. Practice: dc's of a line with ratios 2, 3, 6? [2/7, 3/7, 6/7] Angles 90, 45, 45? [0, 1/sqrt2, 1/sqrt2] dc's of z-axis? [(0,0,1)]

topics.title: Straight Line in Space: Equations and Angle
overview: A straight line in 3D is fixed by a point on it and a direction, or by two points. It can be written in vector form, in Cartesian symmetric form, or in parametric form.
This topic also covers the angle between two lines and the conditions for parallel and perpendicular lines, which are favourite short calculation questions.

terms.meaning: (x - x1)/a = (y - y1)/b = (z - z1)/c, with direction ratios (a, b, c) and point (x1, y1, z1).
r = a + lambda b where a is a position vector of a point and b is the direction vector.
Angle between their direction vectors.
Lines that are neither parallel nor intersecting.

formulas: Vector equation: r = a + lambda b; with a = x1 i + y1 j + z1 k and b = a i + b j + c k.
Cartesian: (x - x1)/a = (y - y1)/b = (z - z1)/c; read the point from the numerators and the dr's from the denominators.
Parametric: x = x1 + a t, y = y1 + b t, z = z1 + c t.
Through two points: direction ratios are (x2-x1, y2-y1, z2-z1).
Angle between lines: cos(theta) = |a1 a2 + b1 b2 + c1 c2|/(sqrt(a1^2+b1^2+c1^2) sqrt(a2^2+b2^2+c2^2)).
Perpendicular lines: a1 a2 + b1 b2 + c1 c2 = 0.
Parallel lines: a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2.
Shortest distance between skew lines r = a1 + s b1 and r = a2 + t b2: |(a2 - a1).(b1 x b2)|/|b1 x b2|.
Coordinate axes as lines: x-axis (x - 0)/1 = y/0 = z/0.
Vector line through two points A and B: r = a + lambda (b - a).
Lines r = a1 + s b1 and r = a2 + t b2 intersect (are coplanar) if (a2 - a1).(b1 x b2) = 0; skew if this is not zero.
Distance between parallel lines r = a1 + s b and r = a2 + t b: |(a2 - a1) x b|/|b|.
how: Given a point and a direction, every point on the line is the point plus a multiple of the direction. Writing the multiple as the same ratio for x, y, z gives the symmetric form.
Reading the Cartesian form back into a vector form just means taking the numerators (with sign changed) as the point and the denominators as the direction.
The angle between two lines equals the angle between their direction vectors, so the dot product formula applies.
A line has two opposite directions, so the line angle is taken as acute and the numerator in the cosine formula is often given with a modulus.
Perpendicularity is dot product zero.
cases: In (x + 5)/3, the point coordinate is -5, not 5, because x + 5 = x - (-5).
Line is uniquely determined by two points (or by a point and a direction); one point alone gives infinitely many lines.
Three non-collinear points determine a plane, not a line.
Parametric form with lambda positive and negative gives the whole infinite line; limited lambda range gives a ray or a segment.
If a denominator is 0, as in (x - 1)/0 = (y - 2)/3 = (z - 3)/4, it means x = 1 on the whole line.
Two lines in 3D can be parallel, intersecting, or skew.
In the perpendicular condition with unknown k, expand the sum of the three products and solve the linear equation for k.
values: Axes as lines: x-axis has direction (1,0,0), y-axis (0,1,0), z-axis (0,0,1), each through the origin.
uses: Describing the path of an aircraft, a cable, or a runway axis.
Finding the angle between two directions such as two routes.
Checking perpendicular or parallel conditions in design problems.
mistakes: Taking the sign of the point coordinates as shown in the equation instead of reversing them.
Using numerators as direction ratios; direction ratios are the denominators.
Dropping the square roots in the magnitudes of the direction ratios, or the rationalisation step.
Dropping a minus sign when multiplying direction ratios such as -3 and 2k.
exam: AAI style: convert the Cartesian form into vector form, find the angle between two lines, or find the constant that makes lines perpendicular. Practice: angle between (x-1)/1 = y/1 = z/0 and x/1 = y/-1 = z/0? [90 degrees]

Direction of line through (1,2,3) and (3,6,9)? [(2,4,6) or (1,2,3)] Lines (x-1)/2 = y/3 = z/k and x/1 = y/2 = (z-1)/(-2) perpendicular: k? [2 + 6 - 2k = 0 so k = 4] Are x/1 = y/2 = z/3 and (x-1)/2 = (y-1)/4 = (z-1)/6 parallel? [Yes]

topics.title: Plane: Equation, Angle and Distance from Point
overview: A plane is a flat surface fixed by a point on it and a normal vector perpendicular to it. Its equation is linear in x, y, z, and the coefficients of x, y, z give the normal direction.
This topic covers equation of a plane, the angle between two planes, and the distance of a point from a plane. These formulas are short and appear frequently in the exam.

terms.meaning: A vector perpendicular to the plane; for ax + by + cz + d = 0 it is (a, b, c).
ax + by + cz + d = 0 with a, b, c not all zero.
Angle between their normals.
Planes with proportional normal vectors.
Shortest distance from a point to the plane, measured along the normal.

formulas: Plane through (x0,y0,z0) with normal (a,b,c): a(x - x0) + b(y - y0) + c(z - z0) = 0.
Vector form: (r - r0).n = 0, or r.n = d where d = r0.n.
Angle between planes: cos(theta) = |n1.n2|/(|n1||n2|) = |a1 a2 + b1 b2 + c1 c2|/(sqrt(a1^2+b1^2+c1^2) sqrt(a2^2+b2^2+c2^2)).
Distance of (x1,y1,z1) from ax + by + cz + d = 0: |a x1 + b y1 + c z1 + d|/sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2).
Distance between parallel planes ax + by + cz + d1 = 0 and ax + by + cz + d2 = 0: |d1 - d2|/sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2).
Perpendicular planes: a1 a2 + b1 b2 + c1 c2 = 0. Parallel planes: a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2.
Intercept form: x/p + y/q + z/r = 1 for intercepts p, q, r on the axes.
Plane through three points: normal = AB x AC.
Angle between a line (direction d) and a plane (normal n): sin(phi) = |d.n|/(|d||n|).
Normal form: r.n_hat = p, where p = |d|/sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2) is the distance of the plane from the origin.
Line with direction d is parallel to the plane if d.n = 0; perpendicular to the plane if d is parallel to n.
Family of planes through the intersection of two planes P1 = 0 and P2 = 0: P1 + k P2 = 0.
how: For any point (x, y, z) on the plane, the vector from the fixed point to it lies in the plane, so it is perpendicular to the normal; this dot product being zero gives a(x - x0) + b(y - y0) + c(z - z0) = 0.
Expanding and combining constants gives the general form.
The angle between planes is the angle between normals because rotating a plane rotates its normal by the same angle.
The point to plane distance is the length of the projection of the vector from any plane point to the given point onto the unit normal, giving the modulus formula.
cases: Plane perpendicular to a line: the line's direction ratios are the plane's normal.
Equation must be in the form with zero on the right before using the distance formula; move the constant first (3x - 4y + 12z = 3 becomes 3x - 4y + 12z - 3 = 0).
Coordinate planes: z = 0 (XY), x = 0 (YZ), y = 0 (ZX); normals are k, i, j.
Plane x = k is parallel to YZ-plane; its normal is along the x-axis.
Always check by substituting the given point into the final equation.
d = 0 means the plane passes through the origin.
If the numerator of the distance formula is 0 the point lies on the plane.
values: Distance of ax + by + cz + d = 0 from the origin is |d|/sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2); for 3x - 4y + 12z = 3 it is 3/13.
Planes x = 0, y = 0, z = 0 are the coordinate planes with normals i, j, k.
uses: Describing surfaces such as a flat runway surface, wall or obstacle limitation surface.
Computing how far an object is from a plane surface.
Finding the angle between two surfaces.
mistakes: Forgetting to take the modulus in the distance formula.
Not moving the constant to the left side before applying the distance formula.
Using the wrong sign for the constant in the plane equation after expanding.
Forgetting the square root of the sum of squares in the denominator.
exam: AAI style: calculate angle between two planes, distance from a point to a plane, or equation of a plane through a point with given normal. Practice: distance of origin from 2x + 3y + 6z = 14? [2] Angle between x + y = 1 and y + z = 1? [60 degrees]
Plane through (1,1,1) with normal (1,2,3)? [x + 2y + 3z = 6] Are 2x - y + z = 3 and x + y - z = 0 perpendicular? [2 - 1 - 1 = 0, yes]

topics.title: LPP Basics: Constraints and Objective Function
overview: Linear Programming deals with optimising (maximising or minimising) a linear function of several variables, subject to a set of linear inequalities. It is the standard tool for allocating limited resources such as labour, material or money.

A Linear Programming Problem (LPP) has three parts: the objective function, the constraints, and the non-negativity restrictions. In the NCERT syllabus only two variables x and y are used, so the problem can be solved graphically.

terms.meaning: The unknown quantities x and y whose values we choose, such as units of each product to make.
The linear function Z = ax + by to be maximised or minimised, with constants a and b.
Linear inequalities or equations in x and y that come from limits on resources.
The conditions x greater than or equal to 0 and y greater than or equal to 0, since quantities cannot be negative.
The set of all points satisfying every constraint including x, y at least 0.
Any point in the feasible region is feasible; the one giving the best Z is optimal.

formulas: General objective function: Z = ax + by, where a and b are constants (no constant term and no powers).
Non-negativity constraints: x greater than or equal to 0, y greater than or equal to 0.
A constraint has form ax + by less than or equal to c, or greater than or equal to c, or equal to c.
Maximisation problem: typically resource constraints of the type less than or equal to.
Minimisation problem: typically requirement constraints of the type greater than or equal to.
Feasible region = intersection of all half-planes given by the constraints.
Z = ax + by = k is a family of parallel lines (iso-profit or iso-cost lines) with slope -a/b.
Standard form for graphing: replace each inequality by equality, draw the line, then test the origin to pick the side.
A feasible region is convex: the segment joining any two of its points lies inside it.
A bounded feasible region is finite in extent; an unbounded one extends indefinitely in some direction.
how: Every real problem is turned into maths in three steps. First pick the decision variables x and y. Second write what is to be optimised as a linear function Z. Third translate each limit into a linear inequality.

The objective function must be linear because profit or cost is proportional to the number of units. A term like x^2 or xy, or a constant added on, would break the linear structure. a constant does not change which point is optimal anyway.
Non-negativity is added because producing a negative number of units is meaningless, and it restricts the region to the first quadrant.
cases: If the feasible region is bounded (closed and enclosed), both a maximum and a minimum of Z exist.
If the feasible region is unbounded, a maximum or minimum may not exist.
If there is no point satisfying all constraints, the region is empty and the problem is infeasible.
If an inequality is strict (less than or greater than), the boundary line is dashed and excluded.
Equality constraints restrict the region to the line itself, not a half-plane.
Constraints x, y at least 0 confine the region to the first quadrant.
values: Standard LPP uses two decision variables x and y; the feasible region lies in the first quadrant.
Slope of the line ax + by = c is -a/b; intercepts are c/a on the x-axis and c/b on the y-axis.
Test point: origin (0,0) satisfies ax + by less than or equal to c when c is positive.
uses: Production planning: units of two products under machine-hour and labour limits.
Diet problems: minimum cost mix meeting nutrient requirements.
Transport and airport scheduling: allocating limited resources such as staff or gates.
mistakes: Writing Z = ax + by + c or Z = x^2 + y as an objective function; an LPP objective is linear with no powers.
Calling x at least 0 and y at least 0 'structural' or 'resource' constraints; they are non-negative constraints.
Forgetting to test the origin when shading an inequality, or shading the wrong side.
Using strict inequality for a closed feasible region.
Drawing the region outside the first quadrant, which ignores the non-negative constraints.
exam: Exam: AAI JE questions ask for the name of x, y at least 0 or the form of the objective function; these are direct recall items.
Practice: What is the name of the function Z = 3x + 4y in an LPP? [Objective function]
Practice: Which quadrant does x, y at least 0 confine the region to? [First quadrant]
Practice: Is Z = 2x^2 + y a valid LPP objective? [No, it is not linear]

topics.title: Corner Point Method and Optimum at Two Points
overview: The corner point method is the standard graphical way of solving an LPP. The feasible region is a convex polygon, and the best value of a linear function Z always occurs at a vertex (corner point) of the region.
A frequent exam twist is that the optimum occurs at two corner points at once. Then Z must have equal values at those two points, which gives a relation between the coefficients p and q.

terms.meaning: A vertex of the feasible region, where two boundary lines meet.
A feasible region that can be enclosed in a circle; it has finitely many corner points.
A region where the line segment joining any two points of it lies fully inside it.
Several optimal points; if two adjacent corners are optimal, every point on the segment between them is optimal.
Z at (x0, y0) is obtained by substituting into Z = px + qy.

formulas: Corner Point Theorem: if the feasible region is bounded, Z has both a maximum and a minimum, each at a corner point.
Method: find corner points, compute Z at each, pick the largest (maximum) and the smallest (minimum).
Unbounded region: compute M, the largest or smallest corner value; check the open half-plane ax + by greater than M (for max) or less than M (for min) against the region.
For a maximum in an unbounded region, M is the maximum only if ax + by greater than M has no common point with the region.
For a minimum in an unbounded region, M is the minimum only if ax + by less than M has no common point with the region.
Optimum at two corners (x1, y1) and (x2, y2): p*x1 + q*y1 = p*x2 + q*y2.
Then every point on the segment joining the two corners also gives the same Z (infinitely many optima).
Slope of Z = px + qy = k is -p/q; optimum at two corners means the iso-line is parallel to the edge joining them.
Corner points are found by solving the equations of two intersecting boundary lines together.
If the optimum exists in any feasible region, it occurs at a corner point.
how: Z is linear, so on any line segment it changes steadily, never turning back. it therefore cannot have a peak in the middle of an edge or inside the region.
Moving the line Z = k across the region, the last point it touches is a vertex (or a whole edge).
If the iso-line becomes parallel to an edge when it leaves the region, it touches the full edge at once, so both end corners tie.
Setting the two Z values equal then gives the required condition, for example p*3 + q*0 = p*1 + q*1 gives 3p = p + q, so q = 2p.
cases: Optimum at one corner: unique optimal solution.
Optimum at two adjacent corners: infinitely many solutions along the edge.
Bounded region: max and min always exist.
Unbounded region: may have neither; use the half-plane test.
Corner points need not be given by intercepts only; solve two boundary equations to find them.
If conditions p, q greater than 0 are given, they prevent trivial solutions such as p = q = 0.
values: Z at a corner (x0, y0) is p*x0 + q*y0.
Two-corner optimum condition is one linear equation in p and q, giving a ratio p : q.
uses: Maximising profit and minimising cost in production, diet and transport models.
Checking whether a solution is unique, or whether the manager has flexibility along an edge.
Finding the profit ratio at which two plans become equally good.
mistakes: Equating Z at corner points that are not both optimal, for example not the pair named in the question.
Substituting coordinates in the wrong order, using x for y.
Forgetting that the maximum and minimum may be at different corners; check the exact one asked.
Simplifying ratios wrongly, e.g. writing q = 3p as p = 3q.
exam: Exam: corner points and a condition such as 'maximum at two points' are given; equate the two Z values and express p in terms of q (or reverse).
Practice: Corner points (0,4), (2,2), (5,0); minimum at (2,2) and (5,0) with Z = px + qy. Relation? [2p + 2q = 5p so 2q = 3p]
Practice: Corner points (0,0), (4,0), (0,3); Z = 5x + 2y. Maximum? [20 at (4,0)]
Practice: Maximum at (6,0) and (0,4) for Z = px + qy. Relation? [6p = 4q, so 3p = 2q]

topics.title: Sample Space, Events and Classical Probability
overview: Probability measures how likely an event is, on a scale of 0 to 1. For random experiments with equally likely outcomes, the classical definition is used: favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes.

This topic builds the language of the whole chapter: sample space, event, simple event, mutually exclusive events and the set notation for 'or' and 'and'. Dice, coins, cards and balls in bags are the usual settings.

terms.meaning: An experiment whose outcome cannot be predicted in advance, though all possible outcomes are known.
The set of all possible outcomes of the experiment.
Any subset of the sample space.
An event with exactly one sample point.
Events that cannot occur together; their intersection is empty.
Events whose union is the whole sample space.

terms.term: P or Q / P and Q
terms.meaning: P union Q (at least one occurs) and P intersection Q (both occur).

formulas: P(E) = n(E)/n(S) for equally likely outcomes.
0 less than or equal to P(E) less than or equal to 1; P(S) = 1; P(empty set) = 0.
Multiplication principle: n dice give 6^n outcomes; n coins give 2^n.
Mutually exclusive: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).
Complement: P(E') = 1 - P(E).
Odds in favour of E = P(E) : P(E'), that is favourable : unfavourable.
Event 'P or Q' = P union Q; event 'P and Q' = P intersection Q; 'not P' = P'.
Two dice: sum 7 can occur in 6 ways out of 36, so probability 1/6.
Two dice sums: sum 2 or 12 has 1 way, sum 3 or 11 has 2 ways, sum 6 or 8 has 5 ways, sum 7 has 6 ways.
Mutually exclusive and exhaustive events have probabilities adding up to 1.
how: Each outcome of the experiment is equally likely, so probability is a simple ratio of counts. Counting total outcomes uses the multiplication principle: the first die has 6 results, and for each of these the second has 6, giving 36.

For 'or' with mutually exclusive outcomes, favourable cases are simply added, because no outcome is counted twice. Words are translated to sets: 'or' becomes union and 'and' becomes intersection, which is the base of all formulas in later topics.
cases: Single die: S = {1,2,3,4,5,6}, 6 outcomes.
Two dice: 36 ordered pairs; (2,3) and (3,2) are different outcomes.
Coin tossed twice: HH, HT, TH, TT.
Simple events are the single points of S; every event is a union of simple events.
Sure event is S itself (probability 1); impossible event is the empty set (probability 0).
Pack of cards: 52 cards, 4 suits of 13, 26 red, 12 face cards, 4 aces.
values: Die: 6 outcomes; two dice: 36; three dice: 216.
Coin: 2 outcomes; three coins: 8.
Cards: 52, with 26 red, 26 black, 12 face cards.
Probability always lies between 0 and 1.
Two dice: 36 outcomes; both show same number in 6 ways, probability 1/6.
uses: Games and gambling, quality control and sampling.
Airport context: probability of delays or baggage events from frequency counts.
Foundation for all further rules: conditional probability, Bayes theorem, distributions.
mistakes: Counting (2,3) and (3,2) as the same outcome for two distinguishable dice.
Adding probabilities for events that are not mutually exclusive.
Dividing by the favourable count instead of the total count of balls.
Confusing union (or) with intersection (and).
exam: Exam: direct counting questions such as total outcomes, balls of a colour, or naming the event type; answers are quick.
Practice: Three dice are thrown; total outcomes? [216]
Practice: A bag has 3 red, 5 green, 2 white balls; P(red or white)? [5/10 = 1/2]
Practice: A die is thrown; P(number at most 2)? [1/3]
Practice: What is the event with no sample point called? [Impossible event]

topics.title: Addition Rule, Complement and Independent Events
overview: This topic covers the probability of 'A or B' when events may overlap, the quick 'at least one' trick using the complement, and independent events where one event does not affect the other.
It is one of the most used toolkits in the chapter: many questions about two persons, two dice or two machines reduce to these few lines.

terms.meaning: A and B are independent if the occurrence of one does not change the probability of the other.
The event 'A does not occur'; P(A') = 1 - P(A).
The event that one or more of the given events occur, which is the complement of 'none occurs'.
Cases that cannot happen together, so their probabilities add.
(A union B)' = A' intersection B', and (A intersection B)' = A' union B'.

formulas: General addition rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B).
For mutually exclusive A, B: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).
Complement: P(A') = 1 - P(A).
Independent events: P(A and B) = P(A)*P(B).
If A, B are independent then A', B and A, B' and A', B' are also independent.
At least one of independent A, B: P = 1 - P(A')*P(B') = 1 - (1 - P(A))(1 - P(B)).
Neither occurs: P(A' and B') = 1 - P(A or B).
Exactly one of two independent events: P(A)*P(B') + P(A')*P(B).
Two dice, at least one shows less than 5: 1 - (2/6)^2 = 8/9.
Three events: P(A or B or C) = P(A) + P(B) + P(C) - P(AB) - P(BC) - P(AC) + P(ABC).
P(A only) = P(A) - P(A and B), the part of A outside B.
Independence of A and B is checked by P(A and B) = P(A)*P(B).
how: Adding P(A) and P(B) counts the overlap twice, so subtract it once; this gives the general addition rule. The union and the 'neither' event together cover the whole sample space, so P(neither) = 1 - P(A or B).

For independent events the joint probability is a product. Contradiction between two speakers means exactly one is truthful: one tells truth and the other lies, two disjoint cases, each a product by independence.
cases: Mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities are NOT independent, because P(A and B) = 0 differs from P(A)*P(B).
Independent events have non-empty overlap in general.
'At least one' is usually easier through the complement 1 - P(none).
'Exactly one' needs two disjoint cases; do not use the complement alone.
Several independent events: P(at least one) = 1 - product of P(each fails).
Percentages must be changed to decimals before multiplying.
values: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) when P(A and B) = 0.
Two dice, both less than 5: (4/6)^2 = 4/9; at least one less than 5 is 1 - 1/9 = 8/9.
uses: Reliability: chance that at least one of several components works.
Two-person statements, witnesses and testimony problems.
Dice and coin games where throws are independent.
mistakes: Treating mutually exclusive as independent, or the reverse.
Multiplying P(A) and P(B) for 'A or B' instead of adding and subtracting the overlap.
Using only one of the two disjoint cases when finding a contradiction.
Computing P(none) as 1 - P(A) - P(B) without checking overlap.
exam: Exam: framed as 'probability of at least one', 'contradict each other' or 'neither occurs' with independent events or dice.
Practice: A hits target with 0.6, B with 0.5, independently; P(at least one hits)? [1 - 0.4*0.5 = 0.8]
Practice: Same A and B; P(exactly one hits)? [0.6*0.5 + 0.4*0.5 = 0.5]
Practice: P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.4, P(A and B) = 0.1; P(A or B)? [0.6]

topics.title: Conditional Probability and Multiplication Rule
overview: Conditional probability is the probability of an event after we already know another event has occurred. The known event acts as the new, smaller sample space.
It leads to the multiplication rule and, with the total probability theorem, to Bayes theorem. It also gives a test for independence.

terms.meaning: Probability of A given that B has already occurred.
The set B, which replaces S once B is known to have happened.
P(A and B) = P(A)*P(B|A) = P(B)*P(A|B).
A, B independent if and only if P(A|B) = P(A).
P(A and B), the probability that both occur.

formulas: P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B), provided P(B) is greater than 0.
P(A and B) = P(A)*P(B|A) = P(B)*P(A|B).
If A and B are independent: P(A|B) = P(A) and P(B|A) = P(B).
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B), used to find the joint probability.
P(A' union B') = 1 - P(A and B) = 1 - P(A)*P(B|A) (De Morgan).
For three events: P(A and B and C) = P(A)*P(B|A)*P(C|A and B).
If A is a subset of B: P(A|B) = P(A)/P(B).
P(A|B) + P(A'|B) = 1, and P(S|B) = 1.
Independence test: P(A and B) = P(A)*P(B) is equivalent to P(A|B) = P(A) when P(B) is positive.
how: Once B is known, only outcomes inside B are possible, so the denominator changes from n(S) to n(B), and favourable cases become those in both A and B. Dividing both counts by n(S) gives P(A and B)/P(B).
Rearranging the formula gives the multiplication rule. For independent events the extra information does not matter, so the conditional probability equals the ordinary one.
A quick check: separate die rolls are independent, so a later throw has probability 1/6 whatever happened before.
cases: If B is a subset of A: P(A|B) = 1.
If A and B are mutually exclusive: P(A|B) = 0.
P(A|B) and P(B|A) are generally different.
Sometimes the conditional value is stated directly: '10 percent of females are graduates' means P(graduate | female) = 0.1.
With coin or children problems, list equally likely outcomes, remove those not allowed by the condition, and count.
Conditional probabilities obey all usual rules, such as the complement rule.
values: Two children or two boxers: 4 equally likely cases; given at least one is a man, 3 remain, so P(both men) = 1/3.
Separate throws of a die are independent, so a later throw stays 1/6 whatever the earlier throws gave.
uses: Medical tests, quality control and sampling without replacement.
Problems with phrases such as 'given that', 'if it is known that' or 'at least one'.
Step toward Bayes theorem and tree diagrams.
mistakes: Swapping the condition: P(A|B) divides by P(B), while P(B|A) divides by P(A); check which event is given.
Using the full sample space instead of the reduced one.
Forgetting the 'at least one' condition removes the FF case, leaving 3 outcomes for two boxers.
Treating dependent events as independent.
exam: Exam: 'find P(A|B)' with data, 'both given at least one', or a statement that two throws are separate.
Practice: Two coins; P(both heads | at least one head)? [1/3]
Practice: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A and B) = 0.2; P(A|B)? [0.5]

topics.title: Bayes Theorem and Total Probability
overview: Bayes theorem reverses a conditional probability. Given the effect (a blue ball drawn, an item found defective), it finds the probability of each possible cause (which urn or which machine).
It uses a partition of the sample space into causes, the total probability theorem for the overall chance of the effect, and the multiplication rule.

terms.meaning: Events E1, E2, ..., En that are mutually exclusive, exhaustive and each with positive probability.
Probability of a cause before the evidence is seen.
Probability of the evidence if cause Ei is true.
Updated probability of the cause after the evidence is seen.
Overall chance of the evidence summed over all causes.

formulas: Total probability: P(A) = sum of P(Ei)*P(A|Ei) over all i.
Bayes theorem: P(Ei|A) = P(Ei)*P(A|Ei) / [sum over j of P(Ej)*P(A|Ej)].
Two causes: P(B|A) = P(B)*P(A|B) / [P(B)*P(A|B) + P(B')*P(A|B')].
Posteriors of all causes add up to 1.
Choosing one of two urns at random: P(urn) = 1/2 each.
Probability of drawing blue from urn with b blue and g green: b/(b + g).
Factory example: defective total = 0.3*0.02 + 0.4*0.03 + 0.3*0.01 = 0.021.
Factory example posteriors: P(A|D) = 0.006/0.021 = 2/7, P(B|D) = 4/7, P(C|D) = 1/7; they add to 1.
Joint probability: P(Ei and A) = P(Ei)*P(A|Ei), the numerator of Bayes theorem.
how: The effect A can arise through any cause, in separate disjoint ways, so P(A) is the sum of P(Ei and A) = P(Ei)*P(A|Ei). That is total probability.

The share of the effect contributed by cause Ei is P(Ei and A)/P(A). This is Bayes theorem. Example: urn B: (1/2)(5/11) = 5/22; urn A: (1/2)(3/7) = 3/14; posterior for B is (5/22)/(5/22 + 3/14) = 35/68. Machine B: 0.012/0.021 = 4/7.
cases: With equal priors, the posterior is proportional to the likelihoods.
A cause with larger prior and larger likelihood has a larger posterior.
Sampling with replacement keeps the likelihoods constant.
A tree diagram shows branches: cause first, then effect; multiply along a branch, add across branches.
Denominator of Bayes is always the total probability of the evidence.
Percentages must be converted into decimals before computing.
values: Equal priors for two urns: each 1/2.
Urn example: P(blue) = 1/2*3/7 + 1/2*5/11 = 34/77, so P(urn B | blue) = 35/68.
uses: Fault diagnosis: which machine produced a defective item.
Medical screening: chance of disease given a positive test.
Spam filtering and any updating of belief from evidence.
mistakes: Using P(blue|urn) as the answer without dividing by total P(blue).
Forgetting to include the prior (1/2 or 30 percent, 40 percent, 30 percent).
Dividing by the sum of priors rather than the sum of products.
Adding unrelated fractions without a common denominator.
exam: Exam: urn or factory problems ending with 'it was found to be ... find the probability it came from ...'.
Practice: Urn 1 has 2 red, 3 black; urn 2 has 4 red, 1 black; urn picked at random; a red ball appears. P(urn 2)? [(4/5)/(2/5 + 4/5) = 2/3]
Practice: Machines A, B make 60 and 40 percent with 1 and 2 percent defects; P(A | defective)? [0.006/(0.006 + 0.008) = 3/7]
Practice: Two causes with posteriors P(E1|A) = 0.35; P(E2|A)? [0.65]

topics.title: Random Variables, Mean and Variance
overview: A random variable assigns a number to each outcome of an experiment. A discrete random variable takes distinct values x1, x2, ..., xn with probabilities p1, p2, ..., pn. This list is the probability distribution.
From a distribution we compute the mean E(X), the variance and the standard deviation, which describe the centre and spread. The weighted mean of grouped data (combined samples) uses the same idea.

terms.meaning: A real-valued function defined on the sample space.
The table of values xi with probabilities pi.
The weighted average of values, sum of xi*pi.
The average squared deviation of X from its mean.
The positive square root of the variance.
The mean of two or more groups, weighted by their sizes.

formulas: Every pi is at least 0, and sum of pi = 1.
Unknown probability: k = 1 - sum of the other probabilities.
Mean: E(X) = sum of xi*pi.
E(X^2) = sum of xi^2*pi.
Variance: Var(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2 = sum of pi*(xi - mean)^2.
Standard deviation = sqrt(Var(X)).
Var(aX + b) = a^2*Var(X); E(aX + b) = a*E(X) + b.
Combined mean = (n1*m1 + n2*m2)/(n1 + n2).
Combined mean lies between the two group means, nearer to the larger group.
Binomial distribution with n trials and success probability p: mean np, variance npq, where q = 1 - p.
Var(X) is at least 0, so E(X^2) is at least [E(X)]^2.
E(constant c) = c and Var(c) = 0.
how: Total probability of all possible values is 1, since exactly one value occurs. This fixes any missing probability. For the given distribution, 0.465 + 0.125 + 0.205 = 0.795, so k = 0.205.
Variance: expand sum of pi*(xi - mu)^2 = sum of pi*xi^2 - 2*mu*sum of pi*xi + mu^2*sum of pi = E(X^2) - 2*mu^2 + mu^2 = E(X^2) - mu^2.
Combined mean: sum of all values equals n1*m1 + n2*m2, and the number of items is n1 + n2. Example: (13*37 + 17*43)/30 = (481 + 731)/30 = 40.4.
cases: Variance is never negative; it is zero only when X is constant.
Adding a constant to X shifts the mean but not the variance.
Multiplying X by a changes the standard deviation by |a|.
Bernoulli trial: values 0 and 1 with probabilities q and p; mean p, variance p*q.
Fair die: mean 3.5, variance 35/12.
Equal group sizes give the simple average of the two means.
values: Sum of all probabilities in a distribution: 1.
Combined mean needs the group sizes as weights.
uses: Statistics of marks and sales, expected profit in decision making.
Expected value of games and insurance.
Combining data from separate samples or shifts.
mistakes: Writing variance as E(X^2) + [E(X)]^2 or [E(X^2)] - E(X) (wrong).
Averaging two means without weights.
Forgetting that the missing probability makes the total 1, not 100.
Taking the square of the sum instead of the sum of squares in E(X^2).
exam: Exam: find the unknown probability, name the variance formula, or combine two sample means.
Practice: P(X = 0, 1, 2) = 0.3, 0.5, k; find k and E(X). [k = 0.2; E(X) = 0.9]
Practice: Means 50 and 60 with sizes 20 and 30; combined mean? [56]
Practice: E(X) = 4 and E(X^2) = 20; variance? [4]

topics.title: Solving linear inequalities in one variable
overview: A linear inequality in one variable compares two linear expressions using less than, greater than, at most or at least. Its solution is a whole set of values, usually an interval on the number line.
This chapter is about rules for manipulating inequalities and writing the answer in interval notation. Every step is mechanical once the sign rules are clear.

terms.meaning: An inequality of the form ax + b less than c (or at most, greater than, at least) where the highest power of the variable is 1.
The set of all values of the variable that make the inequality true, within the stated domain (real numbers, integers or natural numbers).
Writing a solution as (a,b), [a,b], (a,infinity) etc. Round bracket excludes the end point, square bracket includes it.
The number system from which x is allowed to come (R, Z, N). It decides which points of the interval are actually answers.

formulas: Adding or subtracting the same number on both sides keeps the inequality sign unchanged.
Multiplying or dividing both sides by a positive number keeps the sign.
Multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number REVERSES the sign.
ax at most b with a greater than 0 gives x at most b/a; with a less than 0 gives x at least b/a.
To clear fractions, multiply by the LCM of denominators (positive), so the sign stays.
x at least a is [a, infinity); x greater than a is (a, infinity); x at most a is (-infinity, a]; x less than a is (-infinity, a).
Infinity is never included, so it always gets a round bracket.
Combined: a less than x less than b is (a,b); closed version is [a,b].
For a natural-number domain, intersect the real solution with {1,2,3,...}.
Compound inequality: c at most ax + b at most d is solved by doing the same operation on all three parts; divide by a negative number and you must reverse both signs.
If a and b are positive and a less than b, then 1/a is greater than 1/b (reciprocal reverses order for positive numbers).
Two-variable inequality ax + by at most c: draw the line ax + by = c (solid for at most/at least, dashed for strict) and shade the side that satisfies a test point such as the origin.
Solution of a system of inequalities is the intersection of the individual solution sets.
how: An inequality is like a balance that only tips one way. Adding the same amount to both sides moves both pans equally, so the order does not change. Multiplying by a positive number only rescales, so the order stays.

Multiplying by a negative number flips the number line (for example 2 less than 5 but -2 greater than -5), so the order reverses. That is why the sign must be reversed whenever you multiply or divide by a negative number.
Solve by collecting x terms on one side and constants on the other, then divide by the coefficient of x. Finally write the result in interval form and apply the domain.
cases: The x terms cancel and a true statement remains (like 0 less than 3): solution is all of the domain.
The x terms cancel and a false statement remains (like 0 greater than 3): no solution, empty set.
Coefficient of x negative: sign flips at the final division step.
With fractions, multiply every term including the ones without fractions.
Natural-number domain can give no solution even if the real solution exists (for example x at most -7).
For ax + b at most c with a = 0, the result is a plain true or false statement about b and c, so the answer is all of the domain or the empty set.
values: Symbol meaning: at most = less than or equal to; at least = greater than or equal to.
Empty set is written as no solution.
Number line: closed dot for included end point, open dot for excluded.
Union of intervals uses the symbol U; intersection keeps only common points, e.g. (1,5) and [3,8] intersect in [3,5).
uses: Finding feasible ranges in budgets, speed limits and capacity problems.
Base for linear programming and absolute value inequalities in later chapters.
mistakes: Forgetting to reverse the sign when dividing by a negative number.
Using a square bracket with infinity.
Ignoring the domain (natural numbers) and giving a real interval anyway.
Not multiplying a constant term by the LCM while clearing fractions.
Mixing up (a,b) and [a,b] when the inequality is strict or non-strict.
exam: AAI JE questions give a one-variable inequality and ask for the solution interval or the number of natural-number solutions.
Try: Solve 3x - 5 at least 4 over R. [x at least 3, i.e. [3, infinity)]
Try: Solve -2x less than 6. [x greater than -3]
Try: Solve 4x + 3 at most 2x - 1 for x natural. [no solution]
Try: Solve (x-1)/2 at least (x+2)/3. [x at least 7]

topics.title: Word problems on linear inequalities
overview: Many exam questions describe a situation in words, such as cost and revenue or consecutive numbers, and ask when a condition holds. You translate the words into a linear inequality, solve it, and then apply the real-world restrictions.
The skill is translation: pick a variable, write each condition as an inequality, solve, and check the answer makes sense (whole numbers, positive values and so on).

terms.meaning: Total expense as a function of the number of units, for example C = 300 + 1.5x (fixed cost plus variable cost).
Total money received, for example R = 2x for price 2 per unit.
Revenue minus cost; profit is made when revenue is greater than cost.
The quantity where revenue equals cost, so profit is zero.
Odd numbers differing by 2, written x and x+2 with x odd.

formulas: Profit P = R - C; profit exists when R greater than C.
Break-even: R = C gives the boundary; profit for quantity greater than this boundary when revenue per unit exceeds cost per unit.
Linear cost: C = fixed cost + (cost per unit)*x.
Consecutive odd integers: x, x+2 with x odd.
Consecutive integers: x, x+1; consecutive even: x, x+2 with x even.
Sum of two consecutive odd numbers = 2x + 2.
Translate: at least = greater than or equal to; at most = less than or equal to; more than = greater than; less than = less than.
Total must be within a range: lower less than expression less than upper.
Break-even quantity = fixed cost / (price per unit - variable cost per unit); here 300/(2 - 1.5) = 600.
Plan comparison: plan A cheaper than plan B when cost A less than cost B; solve for the quantity where they are equal first.
Average or mean condition: (sum of values)/n at least m means sum at least nm.
Percentage conditions: x percent of y = xy/100; convert to a linear inequality before solving.
how: Define x clearly (units sold, smaller number). Write every condition from the statement as an inequality in x. Solve them separately with the usual sign rules.

Then take the intersection of all conditions together with hidden conditions such as x being odd, positive or a whole number. For cost and revenue, 2x greater than 300 + 1.5x gives 0.5x greater than 300, so x greater than 600.
Always test one value from your answer and one outside it to confirm the direction is right.
Checking an MCQ answer: pair (9,11) has sum exactly 20, so it fails 'sum more than 20'; pair (11,13) has sum 24 and both below 14, so it passes.
cases: Revenue per unit less than cost per unit: profit never happens.
Exactly at break-even the profit is zero, so strict inequality excludes it.
Pair conditions: sum greater than 20 gives x greater than 9, and larger number less than 14 gives x less than 12; with x odd, only x = 11.
Strict versus non-strict: more than means strict, so the boundary value itself fails.
Minimum whole units: if x greater than 600, the least whole number is 601.
Several candidate options in MCQ: test each against all conditions.
Three consecutive odd numbers: x, x+2, x+4 with sum 3x + 6; this is a common extension of the pair problem.
Two-sided limits such as 'between 10 and 20' translate to a compound inequality: 10 less than x less than 20.
values: Break-even for C = 300 + 1.5x and R = 2x is x = 600.
Odd numbers below 14: 1,3,5,7,9,11,13.
uses: Business decisions on how many units to sell to profit.
Choosing between two plans (call plans, taxi fares) by comparing costs.
Age, mixture and number problems in aptitude tests.
mistakes: Using greater than or equal to when the statement says more than.
Forgetting that numbers must be odd, so listing even candidates.
Solving the sum condition but ignoring the upper bound condition.
Treating the break-even value as a profit quantity.
Writing 'less than 14' for both numbers as x less than 14 instead of x + 2 less than 14 for the larger one.
exam: AAI JE gives a cost and revenue pair or a number-pair puzzle with 4 options; verify options by substituting.
Try: Cost 100 + 2x, revenue 3x. Profit when? [x greater than 100]
Try: Two consecutive even positive integers below 10 with sum greater than 11? [(6,8)]
Try: Three consecutive odd positive numbers with sum greater than 20; the smallest such triple? [5,7,9]

topics.title: Ratios, sums of reciprocals, and linear equations
overview: This topic covers questions that use algebra with linear relations: expressing a ratio of formulas for a cuboid, and deciding what kind of solution a linear equation in two variables has.
They test whether you can convert a geometric ratio into a sum of reciprocals and whether you know that one equation in two unknowns has infinitely many solutions.

terms.meaning: S = 2(lb + bh + hl) for sides l, b, h.
V = lbh.
An equation ax + by = c with a and b not both zero; its graph is a straight line.
A pair (x,y) of whole numbers (positive, zero or negative) satisfying the equation.
An equation for which only integer solutions are sought.

formulas: Cuboid: S/V = 2(lb + bh + hl)/(lbh) = 2(1/h + 1/l + 1/b).
If S/V = sqrt(3), the sum of reciprocals = sqrt(3)/2 = sin(pi/3).
ax + by = c has integer solutions if and only if gcd(a,b) divides c.
If (x0,y0) is one integer solution, all are x = x0 + (b/g)t, y = y0 - (a/g)t, g = gcd(a,b), t an integer.
One linear equation in two unknowns has infinitely many real solutions.
Two such equations: unique, none (parallel) or infinitely many (same line).
Cube of side a: S = 6a^2, V = a^3, so S/V = 6/a.
Two equations a1 x + b1 y = c1 and a2 x + b2 y = c2: unique solution if a1/a2 differs from b1/b2; no solution if a1/a2 = b1/b2 differs from c1/c2; infinitely many if all three ratios are equal.
Lateral surface area of a cuboid = 2h(l + b); space diagonal = sqrt(l^2 + b^2 + h^2).
how: For the cuboid, divide each term of the surface area by lbh. Each term lb/(lbh) becomes 1/h and so on, so S/V = 2 times the sum of reciprocals. Then plug in the given ratio.

For 6x + 22y = 14, divide by 2 to get 3x + 11y = 7. Since gcd(3,11) = 1 divides 7, integer solutions exist, for example x = -5, y = 2 since -15 + 22 = 7. The general solution adds multiples of 11 to x and subtracts multiples of 3 from y.
cases: gcd of coefficients does not divide the constant: no integer solution (for example 2x + 4y = 7).
Both coefficients share a factor with the constant: simplify first.
Positive integer solutions may be limited or none even when integer solutions exist.
Cube of side a: S/V = 6/a, sum of reciprocals = 3/a.
sin(pi/3) = sqrt(3)/2, which is why the sum matches option sin(pi/3).
Zero constant: x = y = 0 is always a solution.
Equation 3x + 11y = 7 over real numbers: pick any x and solve for y, so infinitely many real solutions and the graph is a line.
Integer solutions are infinitely many too once one exists: x = -5 + 11t, y = 2 - 3t for any integer t.
values: sin(pi/6) = 1/2, sin(pi/4) = 1/sqrt(2), sin(pi/3) = sqrt(3)/2, sin(pi/2) = 1, sin(pi) = 0.
Cuboid has 6 faces and 12 edges.
sin(0) = 0, cos(0) = 1, cos(pi/3) = 1/2, cos(pi/4) = 1/sqrt(2), cos(pi/6) = sqrt(3)/2.
uses: Geometry ratio problems in mensuration.
Integer solution tests in number theory and coin or stamp puzzles.
Checking consistency of simple linear systems.
mistakes: Forgetting the factor 2 in S/V = 2(sum of reciprocals).
Concluding no integer solution because x or y came out negative.
Saying unique solution for one equation in two unknowns.
Confusing sin(pi/3) with sin(pi/6) values.
Dividing by 2 and then forgetting that the constant must also be divided before testing the gcd condition.
exam: AAI JE gives a geometric ratio and asks for a value expressed as a trig value, or asks about solution type of a linear equation.
Try: Cube side a, S/V = 2. Side a? [3]
Try: Does 4x + 6y = 9 have integer solutions? [No, gcd 2 does not divide 9]
Try: Find one integer solution of 5x + 3y = 1. [x = 2, y = -3]

topics.title: Principle of mathematical induction: basics
overview: Mathematical induction is a method to prove that a statement P(n) holds for every natural number n. It works like a row of dominoes: show the first falls, and show each one knocks the next.
It is used to prove formulas for sums, inequalities and divisibility facts that cannot be checked one by one.

terms.meaning: A claim depending on a natural number n, such as the sum of first n odd numbers equals n^2.
Verification that P(1) (or the first starting value) is true.
The assumption that P(k) is true for some natural number k.
Proving that P(k) true implies P(k+1) true.
By the principle of induction, P(n) is true for all natural numbers n.

formulas: Step 1: show P(1) is true.
Step 2: assume P(k) true, prove P(k+1) true.
Then P(n) holds for all n greater than or equal to 1.
If the base case is n = a, the result holds for all n greater than or equal to a.
Sum of first n natural numbers = n(n+1)/2.
Sum of squares = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6; sum of cubes = (n(n+1)/2)^2.
Sum of first n odd numbers = n^2.
Sum of first n even numbers = n(n+1); sum of first n odd numbers = n^2.
Geometric sum: 1 + r + ... + r^(n-1) = (r^n - 1)/(r - 1) for r not equal to 1.
Inequality example: 2^n is greater than n for all natural n; base case 2 greater than 1, step 2^(k+1) = 2*2^k is greater than 2k, at least k + 1 for k at least 1.
Proof pattern for sum of odd numbers: P(k) gives 1 + 3 + ... + (2k-1) = k^2; add (2k+1) to both sides to get (k+1)^2, which is P(k+1).
how: P(1) true and the implication P(k) gives P(k+1) for every k together generate P(2), then P(3), and so on without end. Both parts are required: the base case starts the chain and the inductive step keeps it going.
Without the base case, a false statement can still satisfy the implication. Without the step, one true case proves nothing about others.
Writing a proof: (1) state P(n); (2) verify P(1); (3) assume P(k); (4) use it to show P(k+1); (5) conclude for all natural n. All five parts are expected in a full-mark answer.
cases: Base case true but step fails: statement may be false for later n.
Step true but base case fails: statement is false for the starting values (for example n = n + 1 style claims).
Start from n = 0 or n = 3 when the claim is for larger n.
Strong induction assumes P(1),...,P(k) true to prove P(k+1).
The step must work for a general k, not just specific values.
Checking many cases is not a proof.
Statement n^2 + n + 41 is prime holds for n = 1 to 39 but fails at n = 40, showing why finitely many checks never prove a claim.
Statement n is less than 100: false for large n, yet the step P(k) implies P(k+1) fails, so induction does not apply.
Statements like P(n): n(n+1) is even work from n = 1; claims such as 2^n greater than n^2 start from n = 5, because the base case must be the first true value.
values: Sum n(n+1)/2: n=4 gives 10.
Sum of squares n=3 gives 14.
Sum of cubes n=3 gives 36.
uses: Proving summation formulas.
Proving divisibility and inequality statements.
Foundation for recursion and algorithm correctness in computer science.
mistakes: Assuming P(k+1) in the proof (circular reasoning).
Checking only the base case.
Using conditions like P(k+1) = P(k) + 1, which is not the principle.
Forgetting to state the conclusion.
Choosing an option such as P(k+1) = P(k) + 1: that is a relation between values, not the induction principle.
exam: AAI JE asks which condition is needed for induction; the answer centres on the base case P(1) plus the step.
Try: Is a statement true for all n if P(1) alone is true? [No]
Try: Sum of first 5 odd numbers? [25]
Try: Sum of first 4 cubes? [100]

topics.title: Divisibility results using induction
overview: A common application of induction is to show that an expression in n is always divisible by a fixed number. The exam gives the expression and asks for a divisor from the options.
The quick approach is to test n = 1, 2, 3 and take the common divisor, then rely on the induction proof for confidence.

terms.meaning: Expression equals m times an integer.
A number dividing every value of the expression for all n.
A product of r consecutive integers is divisible by r factorial; for three consecutive integers it is divisible by 6.
Remainder after division, used to check cases modulo m.
Writing the P(k+1) term as a multiple of the P(k) term plus a part that is obviously a multiple of m.

formulas: n(n+1)(2n+1) = 6 times (1^2+2^2+...+n^2), so divisible by 6.
n(n+1) is always even; n(n+1)(n+2) is divisible by 6.
a^n - b^n is divisible by a - b.
5^n - 5: values 0, 20, 120, 620 are all divisible by 4 and in fact by 20, since 5^n - 5 = 5(5^(n-1) - 1) and 4 divides 5^(n-1) - 1.
Step trick: 5^(k+1) - 5 = 5(5^k - 5) + 20, so a multiple of 4 results.
n^3 - n = (n-1)n(n+1) is divisible by 6.
n^2 + n is divisible by 2.
a^n + b^n is divisible by a + b when n is odd.
10^n - 1 is divisible by 9; 7^n - 1 divisible by 6; 2^(3n) - 1 divisible by 7; 3^(2n) - 1 divisible by 8.
n^5 - n is divisible by 30; n^3 + 2n is divisible by 3.
n^2 - 1 is divisible by 8 for odd n; n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3) is divisible by 24.
how: Assume the expression E(k) is divisible by m. Write E(k+1) = (some multiple of E(k)) + (a term that is obviously a multiple of m). Both parts divisible by m gives E(k+1) divisible by m.
For 5^n - 5: E(k+1) = 5^(k+1) - 5 = 5(5^k - 5) + 20, and 20 = 4*5. Since E(k) is a multiple of 4, so is E(k+1). The base case E(1) = 0 is divisible by 4.
For n(n+1)(2n+1) use sum of squares: the value is 6 times an integer sum, so divisible by 6 for every n.
Alternative proof for n(n+1)(2n+1): among n, n+1 one is even, and among n, n+1, 2n+1 one is a multiple of 3 (check n modulo 3), so 2 and 3 both divide it, giving 6.
cases: Test n = 1 first; zero is divisible by every number, so use n = 2, 3 too.
Common divisor of 6, 30, 84: gcd is 6.
12 fails for n = 2 (value 30), 7 fails for n = 1 (6).
The answer must work for all n, not only some.
Option containing a larger number that fails one case is wrong.
Greatest such divisor may be a multiple of the listed answer; choose from options.
Common divisor is found as gcd of the values for n = 1, 2, 3; for n(n+1)(2n+1) this is gcd(6, 30, 84) = 6, matching the proof.
Check the options one by one: 7 divides none of 6, 30 and 84 completely, so 7 is out immediately.
uses: Quick elimination of options by trying n = 1, 2.
Proving number theory facts in competitive exams.
Check digit and modular arithmetic reasoning.
mistakes: Testing only n = 1 and picking a number that fails n = 2.
Believing a number that divides one value divides all.
Skipping the base case when the value is zero.
Wrong algebra in rewriting E(k+1).
Assuming a divisor that works for n = 1 and 2 must work for all n without a proof or a third test.
exam: AAI JE gives an expression and four candidate divisors; substitute n = 1, 2, 3 to eliminate.
Try: n^3 - n divisible by? [6]
Try: 7^n - 1 divisible by? [6]
Try: n(n+1)(n+2) divisible by? [6]

topics.title: Conditional statements: converse, inverse, contrapositive
overview: Mathematical reasoning deals with statements that are either true or false. A conditional statement has the form if p then q. From it we build related statements by swapping and negating parts.
The exam checks whether you can write the converse, inverse and contrapositive correctly, and know which pairs are logically equivalent.

terms.meaning: A sentence that is definitely true or false, not both.
If p then q, written p implies q; p is the hypothesis and q the conclusion.
not p, which has the opposite truth value of p.
If q then p.
If not p then not q.
If not q then not p.

formulas: Statement: p implies q.
Converse: q implies p.
Inverse: (not p) implies (not q).
Contrapositive: (not q) implies (not p).
A conditional and its contrapositive are logically equivalent.
The converse and the inverse are logically equivalent to each other.
p implies q is false only when p is true and q is false.
Negation of p implies q is p and (not q).
Other wordings of p implies q: p only if q; q if p; p is sufficient for q; q is necessary for p.
p if and only if q is true when p and q have the same truth value (TT or FF), false otherwise.
Contrapositive of the converse is the inverse.
Proof by contradiction: assume the negation of the claim and reach a false statement.
how: To form the inverse, keep the if-then structure and negate both parts in place. To form the converse, swap the parts without negating. The contrapositive does both: swap and negate.

Contrapositive equivalence: if q false forces p false, then p true must force q true, so the two say the same thing. The converse says something different, so it can be false even when the original is true.
Negating a statement: change it to the opposite, for example 'do not have a common point' becomes 'have a common point'; 'parallel' becomes 'not parallel'.
Memory aid for the three forms: converse = swap, inverse = negate, contrapositive = swap and negate. Only the contrapositive always has the same truth value as the original.
cases: Original: if two lines are parallel, they do not have a common point. Inverse: if two lines are not parallel, they have a common point.
Converse of the same: if two lines do not have a common point, they are parallel.
Contrapositive: if two lines have a common point, they are not parallel.
A true statement can have a false converse (if x = 2 then x^2 = 4; converse false).
Biconditional p if and only if q means both p implies q and q implies p.
Careful: not parallel does not always mean intersecting in 3D, but the textbook answer follows the plain negation.
Negating 'for all x, p(x)' gives 'there exists x with not p(x)'; negating 'there exists' gives 'for all, not'.
A tautology is always true (p or not p); a contradiction is always false (p and not p).
values: Truth table of p implies q: TT gives T, TF gives F, FT gives T, FF gives T.
Truth table of p if and only if q: TT gives T, TF gives F, FT gives F, FF gives T.
uses: Proof by contrapositive in algebra and number theory.
Checking logical validity of arguments.
Writing precise conditions in specifications and rules.
mistakes: Mixing up the converse (swap) with the inverse (negate).
Negating only one part of the statement for the inverse.
Thinking the converse is always true.
Changing 'and' or 'or' words when negating simple phrases.
Writing the negation of 'if p then q' as 'if p then not q' instead of 'p and not q'.
exam: AAI JE gives a sentence and asks for its inverse, converse or contrapositive among 4 options.
Try: Converse of 'if it rains, the ground is wet'? [if the ground is wet, it rains]
Try: Contrapositive of 'if x is even then x^2 is even'? [if x^2 is not even then x is not even]
Try: Inverse of 'if a is odd then a^2 is odd'? [if a is not odd then a^2 is not odd]

topics.title: Compound statements and logical connectives
overview: Simple statements can be joined by connectives such as and, or, not to form compound statements. Their truth depends on the truth of the parts.
This topic tests recognising which compound form is described: conjunction, disjunction or negation.

terms.meaning: A single statement with one idea, like Guava is a fruit.
p and q, true only when both p and q are true.
p or q, true when at least one is true.
not p, true when p is false.
A statement made from two or more simple ones by connectives.

formulas: Conjunction: p and q, written p ^ q.
Disjunction: p or q, written p v q.
Negation: not p, written ~p.
p and q true only for (T,T).
p or q false only for (F,F).
De Morgan: not(p and q) = (not p) or (not q).
De Morgan: not(p or q) = (not p) and (not q).
Inclusive or is used in mathematics: p or q includes both true.
Implication p implies q is equivalent to (not p) or q.
Double negation: not(not p) = p.
Distributive laws: p and (q or r) = (p and q) or (p and r); p or (q and r) = (p or q) and (p or r).
Idempotent and commutative laws: p and p = p; p or q = q or p; p and q = q and p.
how: Join the two given statements with the word 'and' for the conjunction, keeping each statement unchanged. If one part is negated in an option, it no longer matches the conjunction of p and q.
With p: Guava is a fruit and q: Rose is a flower, the conjunction is 'Guava is a fruit and rose is a flower'. An option with 'not' or 'or' represents a different compound form.

To build the negation of a compound statement, use De Morgan: negate each part and swap and with or. Example: not(guava is a fruit and rose is a flower) = guava is not a fruit or rose is not a flower.
cases: Both true: conjunction true and disjunction true.
One true one false: conjunction false, disjunction true.
Both false: both false.
Exclusive or is true when exactly one is true (rarely used).
Quantifiers: the negation of 'for all x, p(x)' is 'there exists an x for which p(x) is false'.
Statement with 'not p and q' differs from 'not(p and q)'.
With three statements, the truth table has 8 rows; with n statements, 2^n rows.
Words such as but, however and although act as and in logic.
values: Truth table p,q: TT: and T, or T; TF: and F, or T; FT: and F, or T; FF: and F, or F.
Truth table of not p: p true gives F, p false gives T.
Tautology p or not p is always T; contradiction p and not p is always F.
uses: Constructing and checking logical conditions in programming.
Set theory link: and is intersection, or is union.
Parsing precise statements in rules and contracts.
mistakes: Choosing an option that negates one part as a conjunction.
Reading or as exclusive.
Applying De Morgan without switching and with or.
Confusing the connective with the implication.
Negating 'p and q' as 'not p and not q' instead of 'not p or not q'.
