exam: AAI JE gives p and q and asks which option is the conjunction or disjunction.
Try: Disjunction of p and q above? [Guava is a fruit or rose is a flower]
Try: Negation of p? [Guava is not a fruit]
Try: When is p and q false for p true? [when q is false]

topics.title: Dimensions of physical quantities
overview: The dimension of a quantity expresses how it depends on the base quantities mass M, length L, time T, current A, temperature K. It is written inside square brackets like [M L T^-2].
Dimensions let you identify a quantity, find its unit and check formulas. This topic is a staple of AAI JE style Physics questions.

terms.meaning: Expression showing powers of base quantities in a physical quantity.
A quantity with all powers zero, such as strain, refractive index, angle, ratios.
Independent quantities: mass, length, time, current, temperature, amount of substance, luminous intensity.
A quantity obtained from base quantities using formulas.
Every term in a valid equation has the same dimensions.

formulas: Force: [M L T^-2].
Energy or work: [M L^2 T^-2].
Power: [M L^2 T^-3].
Pressure or stress: [M L^-1 T^-2].
Surface tension = force/length: [M T^-2].
Thermal conductivity k from Q/t = k A (delta T)/x: [M L T^-3 K^-1].
Permeability mu0 from F/L = mu0 I1 I2/(2 pi d): [M L T^-2 A^-2].
Magnetic field B: [M T^-2 A^-1].
Momentum: [M L T^-1]; angular frequency: [T^-1]; moment of inertia: [M L^2].
Torque and angular momentum: torque [M L^2 T^-2]; angular momentum [M L^2 T^-1].
Heat capacity, entropy and Boltzmann constant: [M L^2 T^-2 K^-1].
Charge [A T]; potential difference [M L^2 T^-3 A^-1]; resistance [M L^2 T^-3 A^-2]; capacitance [M^-1 L^-2 T^4 A^2]; inductance [M L^2 T^-2 A^-2].
Magnetic flux [M L^2 T^-2 A^-1]; magnetic moment [L^2 A]; permittivity of free space [M^-1 L^-3 T^4 A^2]; speed of light c = 1/sqrt(mu0 eps0) has [L T^-1].
Young's modulus and bulk modulus: [M L^-1 T^-2]; viscosity coefficient [M L^-1 T^-1]; Stefan constant [M T^-3 K^-4].
Torsion constant = torque/angle: [M L^2 T^-2].
how: Start from a defining formula and replace each quantity by its dimension. For thermal conductivity, Q/t is power [M L^2 T^-3]; k = power times x divided by A times delta T, giving M L^2 T^-3 * L / (L^2 K) = M L T^-3 K^-1.
For mu0, F/L has dimension [M T^-2]. Then mu0 = (F/L)*2 pi d/(I1 I2) = M T^-2 * L / A^2 = M L T^-2 A^-2.
Numbers like 2 and pi and functions like sin have no dimension.
cases: Surface tension and spring constant share dimension [M T^-2].
Strain, angle, refractive index, relative density are dimensionless.
Moment of inertia [M L^2] is not dimensionless.
Surface tension has dimension, so it is not dimensionless.
Torque and energy share dimension [M L^2 T^-2] but are different quantities.
Dimension cannot fix pure numerical constants.
Limits of dimensional analysis: it cannot give pure numbers like 1/2 or 2 pi, cannot handle sums of different terms, and cannot tell scalar from vector.
Exponent and argument of sin, cos, log or exp must be dimensionless, so in e^(kt) the product kt has no dimension.
values: Frequency [T^-1]; velocity [L T^-1]; acceleration [L T^-2].
Impulse [M L T^-1]; density [M L^-3].
Gravitational constant G: [M^-1 L^3 T^-2].
Planck constant h: [M L^2 T^-1].
Specific heat: [L^2 T^-2 K^-1].
Angle, strain, Poisson ratio, refractive index, relative density, Reynolds number and Mach number are all dimensionless.
uses: Identifying quantities from dimension options.
Checking correctness of a formula.
Converting units and deriving relations.
Three uses of dimensional analysis: check a formula, convert units between systems, derive relations between quantities.
mistakes: Forgetting the temperature K in thermal quantities.
Treating surface tension as dimensionless.
Missing the A^-2 in mu0.
Mixing up force dimension with energy.
Mixing up torsion constant [M L^2 T^-2] with surface tension [M T^-2].
exam: AAI JE gives a dimension and asks which quantity has it, or a quantity and asks for its dimension formula.
Try: Dimension of pressure? [M L^-1 T^-2]
Try: Dimension of Planck constant? [M L^2 T^-1]
Try: Dimension of specific heat capacity? [L^2 T^-2 K^-1]

topics.title: SI system, base units and derived units
overview: The SI system is the internationally agreed set of units. It has seven base units and many derived units, plus some units that are accepted for use but are not SI.
Questions ask which quantity or unit belongs to SI and which does not.

terms.meaning: Unit of a base quantity defined independently.
Unit formed by combining base units, such as newton.
Radian is the SI unit of plane angle and steradian of solid angle, both dimensionless.
Units outside SI like litre, hour, bar, though accepted for use.
The reference definition used to realise a unit.

formulas: Seven SI base units: metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol), candela (cd).
Newton N = kg m s^-2; joule J = N m; watt W = J/s.
Pascal Pa = N/m^2; hertz Hz = s^-1.
Coulomb C = A s; volt V = J/C; ohm = V/A.
Litre = 10^-3 m^3 (accepted, not SI).
1 radian is dimensionless.
Tesla T = Wb/m^2 = kg s^-2 A^-1; weber Wb = V s; farad F = C/V; henry H = V s/A; siemens S = A/V.
Lux lx = lm/m^2; becquerel Bq = s^-1; gray Gy = J/kg.
Degree Celsius is accepted with SI; t in degrees C = T in K minus 273.15.
how: SI chooses seven independent quantities and defines their units from fixed natural constants. All other units come as products of powers of these. A unit like litre is a convenient name for 10^-3 m^3 but it is not itself an SI unit.
So check the list of seven base units and the named derived units; anything else like litre, calorie, horsepower or light year is non-SI.
cases: Kilogram is the only base unit with a prefix in its name.
Kelvin is written without a degree sign.
Ampere is the base unit for electrical quantities, not coulomb.
Calorie, horsepower, bar, light year, litre are non-SI.
Angle: radian is SI derived unit.
Mole measures amount of substance.
Since 2019 all seven base units are defined from fixed constants (for example h, c, e, k, and the second from caesium frequency).
Quantities with base unit: length m, mass kg, time s, current A, temperature K, amount mol, luminous intensity cd.
values: SI prefixes: kilo 10^3, mega 10^6, giga 10^9, milli 10^-3, micro 10^-6, nano 10^-9, pico 10^-12.
1 calorie = 4.18 J (approx).
More prefixes: deci 10^-1, centi 10^-2, tera 10^12, femto 10^-15, atto 10^-18.
1 eV = 1.6 x 10^-19 J; 1 angstrom = 10^-10 m; 1 fermi = 10^-15 m; 1 light year = 9.46 x 10^15 m; 1 parsec = 3.08 x 10^16 m.
1 bar = 10^5 Pa; 1 atm = 1.013 x 10^5 Pa; 1 horsepower = 746 W; 1 tonne = 1000 kg.
uses: Choosing consistent units in calculations.
Spotting wrong units in answers.
Understanding data sheets and engineering specifications.
mistakes: Treating litre as an SI unit.
Thinking coulomb is a base unit.
Writing degree Kelvin.
Using gram as the SI base unit of mass.
Treating hour, minute, tonne or electron volt as SI units; they are accepted for use with SI only.
exam: AAI JE asks which of four listed units is not an SI unit or which is a base unit.
Try: Is mole an SI base unit? [Yes]
Try: Which is SI base: newton, ampere, joule? [ampere]
Try: 1 litre in m^3? [10^-3]

topics.title: Errors in measurement and error propagation
overview: Every measurement has an uncertainty. The least count of the instrument sets the smallest error, and when quantities are combined, their errors combine too.
This topic includes absolute, relative and percentage error, and rules for sums, products and quotients.

terms.meaning: Smallest value an instrument can measure; it sets the minimum error.
Size of the difference between measured and true value.
Absolute error divided by the measured value.
Relative error multiplied by 100.
Largest error allowed or expected, often taken as the least count.

formulas: Relative error = (delta a)/a; percentage error = (delta a)/a * 100.
Sum or difference: delta Z = delta A + delta B (absolute errors add).
Product or quotient: (delta Z)/Z = (delta A)/A + (delta B)/B.
Power: Z = A^n gives (delta Z)/Z = n (delta A)/A.
For R = V/I: (delta R)/R = (delta V)/V + (delta I)/I.
Percentage error in the measurement from least count = (LC)/(value) * 100.
Mean absolute error = average of individual absolute errors.
General power law: Z = A^p B^q / C^r gives (delta Z)/Z = p (delta A)/A + q (delta B)/B + r (delta C)/C.
Mean value = sum of readings / n; absolute error of one reading = |reading - mean|.
Vernier least count = 1 main scale division minus 1 vernier division; screw gauge least count = pitch / number of circular scale divisions.
Significant figures: in addition keep the fewest decimal places; in multiplication keep the fewest significant figures.
how: For a quotient R = V/I, take logs: ln R = ln V - ln I. Differentiating gives dR/R = dV/V - dI/I, and in the worst case the errors reinforce, so we add the magnitudes. Hence the sum of relative errors.
Example: V = 100 +- 4 gives 4 percent; I = 10 +- 0.3 gives 3 percent; R has 4 + 3 = 7 percent error.
For the stop watch, the error is the least count 0.5 s on 1.5 s, so 0.5/1.5 = 33.3 percent.
cases: Errors always add for product and quotient, never subtract.
Power n multiplies the relative error by n (for example a square doubles it).
Sum and difference add absolute errors, not relative ones.
Small least count gives small error.
Systematic errors have a fixed direction; random errors vary.
Significant figures follow the least precise number.
Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated readings to each other.
Zero error must be subtracted from the reading; systematic errors include instrument, personal and environmental errors.
A difference of two nearly equal quantities has a large relative error even though the absolute errors add.
values: R = V/I gives 100/10 = 10 ohm with 7 percent error, i.e. 10 +- 0.7 ohm.
Relative error is dimensionless.
Stop watch: reading 1.5 s with least count 0.5 s gives 0.5/1.5 = 1/3, which is 33.3 percent.
uses: Reporting experimental results with uncertainty.
Estimating how reliable a calculated quantity is.
Choosing an instrument for required accuracy.
mistakes: Subtracting relative errors for a quotient.
Forgetting to multiply by the power.
Forgetting to convert the relative error to percent.
Using absolute errors in a product formula.
Using the least count as a percentage directly without dividing by the measured value.
exam: AAI JE gives values with errors and asks for the percentage error in a derived quantity.
Try: Length 10 +- 0.1, width 5 +- 0.1. Percentage error in area? [3 percent]
Try: Radius with 2 percent error; error in volume of sphere? [6 percent]
Try: Least count 0.01 cm on 2.00 cm length: percentage error? [0.5 percent]

topics.title: Vectors, Displacement and Constant-Acceleration Kinematics
overview: Kinematics describes motion without asking what causes it. Position, velocity and acceleration are vectors, so direction and sign matter as much as size. This is the base of the whole Mechanics chapter.

Most exam problems use either vector components (resolving a force or displacement), the equations of uniform acceleration, or reading a graph. Train and bridge style problems are simple uniform-speed cases with unit conversion.

terms.meaning: Straight-line vector from start point to end point; it can be smaller than the distance travelled.
Rate of change of displacement, v = dr/dt; slope of the position-time graph.
Rate of change of velocity, a = dv/dt; slope of the velocity-time graph.
p = m*v, a vector in the direction of velocity; unit kg m/s.
Projection of a vector on an axis: F*cos(angle with that axis).
Motion with constant velocity, so zero acceleration.

formulas: v = u + a*t (u is initial velocity, a constant)
s_n (in the nth second) = u + a*(2n - 1)/2
From r(t): v = dr/dt and a = d^2r/dt^2; r(0) = 0 if the body starts at the origin and dr/dt at t=0 must equal u
Displacement for perpendicular legs a and b: sqrt(a^2 + b^2)
Component of F along a line at angle A to it: F*cos(A); perpendicular component: F*sin(A)
Dot product A.B = Ax*Bx + Ay*By + Az*Bz = |A||B|cos(angle)
Momentum p = m*v; for a constant force from rest p = F*t
Time to cross a bridge or platform = (length of train + length of bridge)/speed
Convert km/h to m/s by multiplying by 5/18
Resultant of two vectors at angle A between them: R = sqrt(P^2 + Q^2 + 2*P*Q*cos(A)); for A = 90 degrees R = sqrt(P^2 + Q^2)
Average speed = total distance/total time; average velocity = total displacement/total time
Relative velocity of A with respect to B: v_AB = v_A - v_B (same direction subtract, opposite directions add)
Unit vector A_hat = A/|A|; magnitude |A| = sqrt(Ax^2 + Ay^2 + Az^2)
Cross product magnitude |A x B| = |A||B|sin(angle); i.j = 0, i.i = 1, i x j = k
Free fall from rest: v = g*t, h = (1/2)*g*t^2, v = sqrt(2*g*h)
how: Each equation of motion comes from integrating a constant acceleration. Since a = dv/dt is constant, v rises linearly with time, giving v = u + a*t. Integrating v once more gives s = u*t + a*t^2/2.
Eliminating t between the two gives v^2 = u^2 + 2*a*s.
For a given position function you can test it by differentiation: the first derivative at t=0 must equal the given initial velocity and the second derivative gives the (constant) acceleration.
A straight line on a position-time graph has a constant slope, hence constant velocity.
A train crosses a bridge only when its tail leaves the bridge, so the front must travel the bridge length plus the train length.
cases: Straight x-t line: constant velocity, zero acceleration; steeper line means greater speed
Curved x-t line: velocity is changing, so acceleration is not zero
Body starting from rest: u = 0, so v = a*t and p = m*a*t
Displacement is zero for a round trip while distance is not
A component is zero when the vector is perpendicular to the chosen line
In a v-t graph, area under the curve gives displacement
Distance is never less than the magnitude of displacement; they are equal only for straight-line motion in one direction
In a v-t graph slope gives acceleration; a horizontal line means zero acceleration
Two vectors give maximum resultant when parallel (angle 0) and minimum when antiparallel (angle 180)
values: Slope of x-t line at 30 degrees: v = tan(30 degrees) = 0.577 (in graph units), not 30
Speed of a train crossing a pole: time = length/speed; 72 km/h = 20 m/s, 54 km/h = 15 m/s, 36 km/h = 10 m/s
uses: Choosing the correct position equation from options by checking initial velocity
Finding momentum and velocity of a body under constant force
Resolving forces and finding resultant displacement in navigation problems
mistakes: Using sin instead of cos: the component along a line uses the angle measured from that same line
Forgetting to add the train length to the bridge length
Not converting km/h to m/s before using seconds
Taking distance instead of displacement
Treating a graph angle as the velocity value: the slope is tan(angle) in graph units, not the angle itself
exam: AAI style: short numerical with one formula and clean numbers.
Practice: a body from rest with a = 2 m/s^2 for 5 s, find s (25 m)
a 100 m train at 36 km/h crosses a 400 m bridge, time? (50 s)
10 N at 30 degrees to horizontal, horizontal component? (8.66 N)
4 m east then 3 m north, displacement? (5 m)

topics.title: Projectile Motion and Free Fall
overview: A projectile moves under gravity alone. Its horizontal and vertical motions are independent: horizontal velocity stays constant while vertical motion has constant acceleration g downward. Free fall and upward throw are the vertical-only special case.
This topic links vectors with kinematics and is a favourite for questions on range, maximum height, time of flight and the value of acceleration at the top of the path.

terms.meaning: Body thrown into the air that moves only under gravity (air resistance ignored).
Horizontal distance covered when the body returns to launch level.
Total time in air until it returns to launch level.
Greatest vertical height reached, where vertical velocity is zero.
Acceleration due to gravity, about 9.8 m/s^2 (10 in many problems), always directed downward.

formulas: Components: u_x = u*cos(theta), u_y = u*sin(theta)
v_x = u*cos(theta) (constant); v_y = u*sin(theta) - g*t
x = u*cos(theta)*t; y = u*sin(theta)*t - (1/2)*g*t^2
Time of flight T = 2*u*sin(theta)/g
Maximum height H = u^2*sin^2(theta)/(2*g) = u_y^2/(2g)
Range R = (u^2/g)*sin(2*theta)
Maximum range R_max = u^2/g at theta = 45 degrees
At any height h: v_y^2 = u_y^2 - 2*g*h
Trajectory: y = x*tan(theta) - g*x^2/(2*u^2*cos^2(theta)), a parabola
R = 4*H/tan(theta); for 45 degrees R = 4H
Upward throw: v = u - g*t, max height u^2/(2g), time up = u/g
Free fall from rest: v = g*t, h = (1/2)*g*t^2, v = sqrt(2*g*h)
Horizontal projection from height h with speed u: time t = sqrt(2*h/g), range = u*sqrt(2*h/g)
Speed at any instant: v = sqrt(v_x^2 + v_y^2); direction tan(phi) = v_y/v_x
Time to reach the top t = u*sin(theta)/g, equal to half of T
Range for complementary angles: R(theta) = R(90 - theta)
how: Gravity acts only vertically, so it changes only v_y. Horizontal velocity is therefore unchanged for the whole flight. At the top v_y = 0, which gives t = u_y/g and H = u_y^2/(2g).
Time of flight is twice the time to the top (symmetry), T = 2*u*sin(theta)/g. Range is horizontal speed times T: R = u*cos(theta)*2*u*sin(theta)/g = u^2*sin(2*theta)/g.

The velocity at any point is the vector sum of the constant horizontal part and the changing vertical part. If at a known height both components are given, v_y^2 = u_y^2 - 2*g*h recovers the launch vertical speed.
cases: Angles theta and (90 - theta) give the same range
Horizontal projection from a height: time depends only on height, t = sqrt(2h/g)
At the highest point velocity is horizontal (u*cos(theta)) and acceleration is still g downward
Speed is minimum at the top and equal at equal heights on the way up and down
Vertical throw: speed on return to start equals launch speed, direction reversed
Sign: with up positive, a = -g throughout, even when the ball is momentarily at rest
Max height is largest for vertical throw (theta = 90 degrees) and range is zero there
A body dropped and one thrown horizontally from the same height reach the ground together
values: g = 9.8 m/s^2 (use 10 if the question says so)
sin(2*theta) is maximum (1) at 45 degrees
Range for 30 and 60 degrees are equal
At 45 degrees R_max = u^2/g and H = R/4; with u = 20 m/s and g = 10 R_max = 40 m
uses: Finding the maximum height from velocity measured at some height
Judging acceleration at the top of a throw
Range and time of flight in sports and artillery style cases
mistakes: Saying acceleration is zero at the highest point: it is -g
Using the horizontal speed in the vertical equation
Using sin(theta) in the range formula instead of sin(2*theta)
Forgetting that v_y at the given height is not the launch vertical speed
exam: AAI style: conceptual (acceleration at top) or one-step formula.
Practice: u = 20 m/s at 30 degrees, g = 10, range? (34.6 m)
same, max height? (5 m)
ball thrown up at 20 m/s, time to return? (4 s)
acceleration of a stone at its top point? (g downward)

topics.title: Newton's Laws, Connected Bodies and Momentum Conservation
overview: Newton's laws link force to motion. The first law defines inertia, the second gives F = m*a, and the third says forces come in equal and opposite pairs. For systems of several bodies we apply the second law to each body or to the whole system.
Momentum conservation follows from these laws and is the quickest tool for recoil, explosion and collision problems when no external force acts.

terms.meaning: Tendency of a body to keep its state of rest or uniform motion.
Vector sum of all forces on the body; it alone decides acceleration.
Pulling force transmitted along a string; same throughout a light string.
p = m*v; the net force equals the rate of change of momentum.
One with zero net external force, so total momentum is conserved.

formulas: First law: if net force = 0 then velocity is constant
Second law: F_net = m*a (equivalently F = dp/dt)
Third law: F_AB = -F_BA, acting on different bodies
Chain pulled by F on total mass M: a = F/M
Tension in a string = (mass behind the string, away from the pull) * a
Hanging block m2 pulling trolley m1 with friction: a = (m2*g - mu*m1*g)/(m1+m2), T = m2*(g - a)
Conservation: m1*u1 + m2*u2 = m1*v1 + m2*v2 when F_ext = 0
Recoil: v_recoil = -(m_small*v_small)/M_big
Impulse J = F*t = change in momentum
Weight W = m*g
Atwood machine: a = (m1 - m2)*g/(m1 + m2), T = 2*m1*m2*g/(m1 + m2)
Apparent weight in a lift: N = m*(g + a) going up with acceleration a, N = m*(g - a) going down with acceleration a
Elastic collision in one dimension: v1 = ((m1 - m2)*u1 + 2*m2*u2)/(m1 + m2); for equal masses velocities exchange
Perfectly inelastic collision: common velocity v = (m1*u1 + m2*u2)/(m1 + m2)
Block on smooth incline: a = g*sin(theta), normal reaction N = m*g*cos(theta)
how: Uniform velocity means no acceleration, so by F = m*a the net force is zero. A force is needed only to change velocity, or to cancel friction. On a frictionless table nothing opposes motion, so no force is needed.

For a chain of blocks, all move with the same acceleration a = F/M_total. A string must accelerate every block on its far side, so its tension is the sum of those masses times a. This is why tension grows toward the pulled end.

For recoil, the internal forces are equal and opposite, so total momentum stays at its initial value (zero if everything starts at rest). Then each body's momentum is equal and opposite, and the heavier body gets the smaller speed.
cases: Constant velocity: net force zero (no force needed on frictionless surface)
Chain of blocks: tension nearest the pull is largest
Atwood or table-pulley systems: treat the string as inextensible, same a for both bodies
Starting from rest: total momentum zero, so speeds are in inverse ratio of masses
Elastic collision conserves kinetic energy too; inelastic does not
Negative sign in velocity just means opposite direction
Lift at constant velocity or free-falling: apparent weight is m*g, or zero for free fall
Two blocks in contact pushed by F: contact force on the second block = F*m2/(m1 + m2)
values: Weight of 1 kg = 9.8 N (10 N if g = 10)
Unit of force: newton = kg m/s^2
Unit of momentum: kg m/s
uses: Recoil of a person throwing an object on ice
Tension in coupled wagons or trains
Rockets and guns based on momentum conservation
mistakes: Thinking a force is needed to keep a body moving at constant speed
Using the whole mass for tension instead of only the mass behind the string
Dropping the negative sign of recoil velocity
Forgetting to subtract friction before dividing by total mass
Treating action and reaction as acting on the same body, so they appear to cancel
exam: AAI style: direct numerical or concept (net force at constant velocity).
Practice: 10 kg and 20 kg in contact, pushed by 60 N, a? (2 m/s^2)
50 kg man throws 1 kg at 10 m/s on ice, recoil? (0.2 m/s backward)
two-block chain 2 kg and 3 kg pulled by 10 N, tension between? (4 N)
force to move 5 kg at constant speed on smooth floor? (0 N)

topics.title: Friction and Circular Motion on a Level Road
overview: Friction is the contact force that opposes relative or attempted motion. It comes in static, limiting and kinetic forms, and its behaviour differs for each. On a flat circular road, static friction supplies the centripetal force needed to turn a car.
Together these topics test whether you know that static friction adjusts itself, and that maximum safe speed depends on mu and radius but not on mass.

terms.meaning: Self-adjusting force that equals the applied force until the limit is reached.
Maximum static friction, f_max = mu_s*N.
Friction when sliding, f_k = mu_k*N, usually less than limiting friction.
Net inward force m*v^2/R needed for circular motion.
Ratio of friction to normal reaction; a pure number.

formulas: Static: f_s is less than or equal to mu_s*N, and f_s = applied force while the body is at rest
Kinetic: f_k = mu_k*N
On a level surface N = m*g
Centripetal force F_c = m*v^2/R = m*omega^2*R
Maximum speed on a flat road: m*v^2/R = mu*m*g, so v_max = sqrt(mu*R*g)
Banked road without friction: tan(theta) = v^2/(R*g)
Banked road with friction: v^2 = R*g*(tan(theta) + mu)/(1 - mu*tan(theta))
Angle of repose: tan(theta) = mu
Acceleration on rough incline: a = g*(sin(theta) - mu*cos(theta))
Stopping distance with braking: s = v^2/(2*mu*g)
Angle of friction: tan(lambda) = mu, so lambda equals the angle of repose
Block on a rough incline just about to slide: tan(theta) = mu_s
Minimum force to pull a block on a level rough surface at best angle: F = mu*m*g/sqrt(1 + mu^2)
Maximum speed on a banked road without friction: v = sqrt(R*g*tan(theta))
Time period of circular motion T = 2*pi*R/v; omega = v/R
Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction
how: If a block does not move, its acceleration is zero, so net horizontal force is zero: static friction equals the applied force exactly, whatever its value up to f_max. It becomes mu*N only at the point of slipping.
A car turning on a flat road has no other horizontal force than friction pointing to the centre. Setting mu*m*g = m*v^2/R, the mass cancels, giving v_max = sqrt(mu*R*g).
If speed exceeds this, friction cannot supply enough inward force and the car skids outward.
cases: Applied force less than f_max: block at rest, friction equals applied force
Applied force just reaches f_max: motion about to start
Once sliding, friction drops to the kinetic value
Heavier car or lighter car: same v_max on a flat road
Wet road means smaller mu, so smaller safe speed
Banking reduces dependence on friction; at the design speed friction is zero
Friction on an incline uses N = m*g*cos(theta), not m*g
Static friction on a car tyre rolling without slipping is what actually accelerates and turns the car
values: Typical mu: rubber on dry road about 0.7 to 1, ice near 0.05
mu_s is greater than mu_k
Friction is independent of contact area (for ordinary surfaces)
uses: Safe turning speed on highways and airport taxiways
Stopping distance of vehicles
Deciding if a pushed block will move
mistakes: Using f = mu*N when the body is at rest below the limit
Believing v_max depends on mass
Writing v_max = sqrt(mu*R/g) with g in the denominator
Ignoring that friction acts along the surface, N perpendicular to it
exam: AAI style: concept plus one-line calculation.
Practice: 10 kg block, mu_s = 0.5, g = 10, pushed with 30 N, friction? (30 N, no motion)
max force before slipping? (50 N)
car on R = 40 m, mu = 0.4, g = 10, v_max? (12.6 m/s)
skid distance from 20 m/s with mu = 0.5, g = 10? (40 m)

topics.title: Work, Energy and Power
overview: Work measures energy transferred by a force over a displacement. Kinetic energy is energy of motion, potential energy is stored energy due to position. The work-energy theorem links them, and power gives the rate of doing work.
These are the most frequently tested formulas in Mechanics because most problems reduce to one line of energy accounting.

terms.meaning: W = F.s = F*s*cos(theta); a scalar measured in joules.
Gravitational U = m*g*h, taken relative to a chosen zero level.
Rate of doing work; unit watt = joule per second.
One whose work depends only on end points, such as gravity.

formulas: W = F*s*cos(theta)
Work-energy theorem: W_net = change in K = (1/2)*m*(v^2 - u^2)
Gravitational PE change = m*g*h (fall reduces PE by this amount)
Average power P = W/t
Instantaneous power P = F.v = F*v*cos(theta); with components P = Fx*vx + Fy*vy + Fz*vz
Spring energy U = (1/2)*k*x^2
Conservation of mechanical energy: K + U = constant (conservative forces only)
Resistive force on a stopping body: F = (1/2)*m*u^2/s
Efficiency = useful output/input
Momentum and energy: K = p^2/(2m)
Work by a variable force = integral of F dx = area under the F-x graph
Kinetic energy and speed: K = (1/2)*m*v^2; doubling speed makes K four times
Spring work from x1 to x2 = (1/2)*k*(x2^2 - x1^2)
Power of an engine moving at constant speed v against resistance F: P = F*v
Elastic collision conserves both momentum and kinetic energy; inelastic conserves only momentum
Escape and falling: speed after falling height h from rest v = sqrt(2*g*h)
how: Work done by a net force changes the speed. Since F = m*a and v^2 - u^2 = 2*a*s, multiplying by m/2 gives F*s = (1/2)*m*v^2 - (1/2)*m*u^2. That is the work-energy theorem, and it handles bullets stopped in wood without needing time.
Lifting a body slowly through height h needs work m*g*h, stored as potential energy; falling returns the same amount as kinetic energy. Power for a climbing person is this work divided by time taken.
For a force and velocity that are both vectors, the instantaneous rate of work is the dot product, so only the part of force along velocity delivers power. A perpendicular component does no work.
cases: Work is zero if force is perpendicular to displacement (centripetal force, normal force)
Work by friction is negative; work by gravity is negative when going up
Area under a force-displacement graph = work
Work depends on the frame of reference; kinetic energy is never negative
Power can be negative when the force opposes velocity
Height must be in metres: 50 cm = 0.5 m
values: Joule = N m = kg m^2/s^2
Watt = J/s; 1 kW = 1000 W
1 horse power = 746 W
Typical: lifting 1 kg by 1 m with g = 10 needs 10 J
uses: Stopping force of bullets and brakes
Power rating of lifts, climbers and engines
Energy bookkeeping for falling bodies and springs
mistakes: Using cm instead of m in m*g*h
Forgetting the negative sign of dot-product terms such as -2*1
Mixing average and instantaneous power
Using kinetic energy as m*v^2 without the half
exam: AAI style: direct substitution. Practice: 2 kg dropped 5 m, g = 10, PE lost? (100 J); 1000 kg car at 20 m/s, K? (200000 J); 50 kg climbs 10 m in 20 s, power? (250 W); F = 3i+4j N, v = 2i+1j m/s, P? (10 W)

topics.title: Moment of Inertia and Theorems
overview: Moment of inertia I is the rotational analogue of mass: it tells how hard it is to change the rotation about a particular axis. It depends on mass and on how that mass is distributed relative to the axis.
Standard results for ring, disc, rod and sphere are asked directly, together with the parallel and perpendicular axis theorems.

terms.meaning: I = sum of m*r^2 about an axis; unit kg m^2.
k with I = M*k^2.
I = I_cm + M*d^2 for an axis parallel to one through the centre of mass.
For a planar body I_z = I_x + I_y, axes x and y in the plane.
tau = I*alpha, the rotational form of Newton's second law.

formulas: Ring about axis through centre perpendicular to plane: M*R^2
Ring about a diameter: (1/2)*M*R^2
Ring about a tangent in its plane: (3/2)*M*R^2
Disc about centre perpendicular to plane: (1/2)*M*R^2
Disc about a diameter: (1/4)*M*R^2
Thin rod about centre: M*L^2/12; about one end: M*L^2/3
Solid sphere about diameter: (2/5)*M*R^2; hollow sphere: (2/3)*M*R^2
Parallel axis: I = I_cm + M*d^2
Perpendicular axis: I_z = I_x + I_y
Rotational KE = (1/2)*I*omega^2; angular momentum L = I*omega
Solid cylinder or disc about its axis: (1/2)*M*R^2; hollow cylinder: M*R^2
Solid sphere about a tangent: (7/5)*M*R^2; hollow sphere about a tangent: (5/3)*M*R^2
Rod about an axis through one end perpendicular to it: M*L^2/3 (parallel axis from M*L^2/12 + M*(L/2)^2)
Rectangular plate about centre perpendicular to plane: M*(a^2 + b^2)/12
Rolling without slipping: total K = (1/2)*M*v^2*(1 + k^2/R^2), acceleration on incline a = g*sin(theta)/(1 + k^2/R^2)
Angular equations: omega = omega0 + alpha*t, theta = omega0*t + (1/2)*alpha*t^2, v = omega*R
how: For a thin ring every bit of mass is at distance R from the centre, so about the central perpendicular axis I_z = M*R^2. By symmetry any two perpendicular diameters have equal I, I_x = I_y.
The perpendicular axis theorem then gives I_z = I_x + I_y = 2*I_diameter, so I_diameter = M*R^2/2. The same logic gives (1/4)*M*R^2 for a disc about a diameter.
The parallel axis theorem shifts the axis away from the centre of mass and always increases I, which is why the tangent value (3/2)*M*R^2 is the diameter value plus M*R^2.
cases: Mass concentrated far from axis gives larger I (ring larger than disc of same M and R)
Same body has different I for different axes
Perpendicular axis theorem works only for flat (planar) bodies
Parallel axis theorem needs one axis through the centre of mass
I is additive for bodies about the same axis
Rolling bodies: ring reaches the bottom of an incline last, solid sphere first
Angular momentum is conserved when net external torque is zero (skater pulling arms in spins faster)
Radius of gyration k = sqrt(I/M); for a ring about its centre k = R
values: Ring: MR^2, MR^2/2 (diameter), 3MR^2/2 (tangent in plane), 2MR^2 (tangent perpendicular to plane)
Solid sphere 2/5, hollow sphere 2/3 of M*R^2
uses: Flywheels and rotating machinery
Predicting which body rolls faster down a slope
Angular momentum and spinning skaters
mistakes: Using M*R^2 for the diameter axis
Applying the perpendicular axis theorem to a solid sphere
Using the parallel axis theorem when neither axis passes through the centre of mass
Confusing disc and ring values
Forgetting that the parallel axis theorem uses distance squared, M*d^2, and the centre-of-mass value as the base
exam: AAI style: recall of ring or disc value. Practice: disc about a diameter? (MR^2/4); ring about a tangent in its plane? (3MR^2/2); rod of M and L about one end? (ML^2/3); ring M = 2 kg, R = 0.5 m, about a diameter? (0.25 kg m^2)

topics.title: Fluid Pressure, Depth and Pascal's Law
overview: Pressure is force per unit area. In a fluid at rest it acts equally in all directions and rises with depth. Pascal's law says any pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished everywhere, which is how hydraulic lifts work.
Questions ask for pressure at a depth, depth for a given pressure, or the pressure needed in a hydraulic system where pistons sit at different heights.

terms.meaning: P = F/A; unit pascal (Pa = N/m^2).
Pressure above atmospheric, rho*g*h.
P_atm + gauge pressure.
Pressure change in an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally to every point.
rho = mass/volume; water 1000 kg/m^3.

formulas: P = F/A
Pressure at depth h: P = P_atm + rho*g*h
Gauge pressure = rho*g*h
Pressure difference between two points in a fluid: delta P = rho*g*(h2 - h1)
Hydraulic lift: F1/A1 = F2/A2, so F2 = F1*(A2/A1)
With height difference H between pistons: P_small = W/A_big + rho*g*H (small piston lower)
Buoyant force = rho_fluid*V*g (Archimedes)
Barometer: P = rho_Hg*g*h
Floating body: weight of body = weight of liquid displaced; fraction submerged = rho_body/rho_liquid
Apparent weight in liquid = true weight - buoyant force
Manometer: P_gas = P_atm + rho*g*h (open-tube difference in height h)
Absolute pressure in n atmospheres of total pressure means gauge = (n - 1)*P_atm
how: Consider a vertical column of fluid of height h and base area A. Its weight is rho*A*h*g, which presses on the base, so extra pressure is rho*g*h. Add atmospheric pressure at the surface to get the absolute value.

In a hydraulic lift the pressure in the fluid is the same at the same level. The big piston must be balanced by pressure W/A_big at its level; the smaller piston, being lower, must bear this plus the oil column rho*g*H between the levels.
Pressure at a depth depends only on depth, density and g, not on the shape or width of the container.
cases: Same level in the same fluid means same pressure
Pressure is a scalar though force on a wall is a vector
To have total pressure of n atmospheres, gauge pressure is (n - 1) atmospheres
Ocean bottom pressure is often quoted as gauge (rho*g*h) when atmosphere is ignored
Deeper in denser fluid gives more pressure
Mechanical advantage of lift = A2/A1
Body denser than the liquid sinks, equal density floats fully immersed, less dense floats partly out
Pressure at the bottom of a tank is rho*g*h whatever the shape (hydrostatic paradox)
values: Water density 1000 kg/m^3; mercury 13600 kg/m^3
10 m of water is about 1 atm
1 atm = 10^5 Pa roughly; 10 N/cm^2 when given so in the problem
Atmospheric pressure 76 cm Hg = 760 mm Hg = 1.013*10^5 Pa; 1 bar = 10^5 Pa
Seawater density about 1025 kg/m^3
uses: Hydraulic jacks, brakes and lifts
Diving depth and dam wall design
Barometers and manometers
mistakes: Using total 3 atm in rho*g*h instead of 2 atm gauge
Mixing N/cm^2 with N/m^2
Ignoring the height difference between pistons
Using the surface area A of the wrong piston
exam: AAI style: direct substitution.
Practice: gauge pressure at 10 m in water, g = 10? (10^5 Pa)
depth where gauge pressure is 2 atm of 10^5 Pa, g = 10? (20 m)
small piston 10 cm^2, big 1000 cm^2, force 50 N, lift? (5000 N)

topics.title: Bernoulli's Principle and Aerodynamic Lift
overview: Bernoulli's principle is energy conservation for a flowing ideal fluid. Where the speed is higher the pressure is lower at the same height. It explains how a wing creates lift and how sprays and atomisers work.
Airport operations questions use it for lift on wings: the pressure difference times wing area balances the weight in level flight.

terms.meaning: Incompressible, non-viscous, steady (streamline) flow.
Path followed by a fluid particle in steady flow.
Net upward force from pressure difference across the wing.

formulas: Bernoulli: P + (1/2)*rho*v^2 + rho*g*h = constant
Same height: P1 + (1/2)*rho*v1^2 = P2 + (1/2)*rho*v2^2
Pressure difference: delta P = (1/2)*rho*(v_upper^2 - v_lower^2)
Lift = delta P * wing area
Level flight: Lift = m*g, so m = delta P*A/g
Continuity: A*v = constant
Torricelli speed of efflux: v = sqrt(2*g*h)
Venturi: P1 - P2 = (1/2)*rho*(v2^2 - v1^2)
Convert km/h to m/s: multiply by 5/18
Bernoulli with height change: P1 + (1/2)*rho*v1^2 + rho*g*h1 = P2 + (1/2)*rho*v2^2 + rho*g*h2
Volume flow rate Q = A*v; mass flow rate = rho*A*v
Magnus effect: a spinning ball curves because of pressure difference across it
how: Take a small fluid element moving along a streamline. Work done by pressure forces equals the change in its kinetic and potential energy. Dividing by volume gives P + rho*v^2/2 + rho*g*h constant.
Over a wing, air above moves faster than below, so pressure above is lower. Net upward force is delta P times area. In steady level flight lift equals weight, giving the mass of the plane.
cases: Faster flow: lower pressure (at same height)
Total wing area includes both wings: A = 2*20 = 40 m^2 in the usual question
Streamline flow only; turbulence breaks the law
Horizontal pipe narrowing: speed up, pressure drop
Lift greater than weight: plane climbs; less: it descends
Free surface open to air gives efflux speed sqrt(2gh)
Equation of continuity: narrower section gives higher speed
Bernoulli assumes no viscosity and no change in density, so it fails for turbulent or compressible flow at high speed
values: Air density about 1.2 kg/m^3 at sea level (1 in the problem)
g = 9.8 m/s^2 here
uses: Aircraft wing lift
Carburettors, sprayers, Venturi meters
Why roofs lift in a storm
mistakes: Forgetting to convert km/h to m/s
Using area of one wing only
Writing (v_upper - v_lower)^2 instead of the difference of squares
Using g = 10 when the key uses 9.8
exam: AAI style: lift or mass of a plane from speeds. Practice: v_upper 75, v_lower 55 m/s, rho 1, find delta P? (1300 Pa); same with 40 m^2, lift? (52000 N); water efflux 5 m below surface, g = 10? (10 m/s); pipe area halves, speed? (doubles)

topics.title: Viscosity and Newton's Law of Viscous Force
overview: Viscosity is the internal friction of a fluid, resisting relative motion of its layers. Thick liquids like honey have high viscosity; gases and water have low values.
A plate moving on a thin liquid film is the standard model, and the force needed to keep it moving follows Newton's law of viscosity.

terms.meaning: Property of a fluid by which it resists flow between layers.
Viscous force per unit area per unit velocity gradient; unit Pa s.
dv/dx, change of speed across the fluid layer.
Drag on a small sphere in fluid, F = 6*pi*eta*r*v.
Constant speed when weight equals buoyancy plus drag.

formulas: F = eta*A*(dv/dx)
For thin film of thickness d: F = eta*A*v/d, so eta = F*d/(A*v)
Stokes: F = 6*pi*eta*r*v
Terminal velocity: v_t = 2*r^2*(rho - sigma)*g/(9*eta)
Poiseuille: Q = pi*P*r^4/(8*eta*L)
Reynolds number R_e = rho*v*D/eta; below about 1000 laminar, above about 2000 turbulent
1 kgf = 9.8 N (take 10 if instructed)
SI unit of eta is Pa s = N s/m^2; CGS is poise; 1 poise = 0.1 Pa s
Dimensions of eta: M L^-1 T^-1
Reynolds number: below about 1000 laminar, above about 2000 turbulent, in between unstable
Terminal velocity of a falling sphere in a liquid is reached when weight = buoyancy + 6*pi*eta*r*v
Viscous force on the plate acts opposite to its motion and equals the applied force at constant speed
how: Layers of fluid touching the plate move with it, while the layer at the bottom is at rest. Speed changes linearly over thickness d, so gradient = v/d. The drag on the plate is proportional to area and to this gradient, with eta as the constant.
To move the plate at constant speed, the applied force must balance the viscous force, so eta = F*d/(A*v). Convert force from kgf to N and thickness from mm to m.
cases: Liquids: viscosity falls as temperature rises; gases: it rises
Ideal fluid has zero viscosity
Larger area or smaller gap needs more force
Terminal velocity larger for bigger radius (as r^2)
Laminar versus turbulent decided by Reynolds number
Viscous force acts opposite to relative motion
For the plate problem, the bottom layer is at rest and the top layer moves with the plate, so the gradient is v/d
values: Water at 20 C: about 10^-3 Pa s
Glycerine about 1.4 Pa s
Air about 1.8*10^-5 Pa s
1 poise = 0.1 Pa s; 1 centipoise = 10^-3 Pa s, close to water at 20 C
1 kgf = 9.8 N, usually rounded to 10 N when the problem says so; check the options for which was used
uses: Lubrication of machines
Raindrop and sedimentation speeds
Blood flow and pipelines
mistakes: Not converting kgf to N
Using mm as m for d
Mixing up F = eta*A*v/d with d in the numerator
Confusing poise with Pa s
exam: AAI style: substitution with unit conversion. Practice: F = 0.1 N, d = 0.2 mm, A = 0.2 m^2, v = 0.075 m/s, eta? (1.33*10^-3 Pa s); 1 poise in Pa s? (0.1); doubling the gap, force? (halves); dimensions of eta? (M L^-1 T^-1)

topics.title: Elasticity: Strain and Poisson's Ratio
overview: When a wire is stretched it lengthens along the force and thins across it. Stress and strain describe this, and elastic constants relate them. Poisson's ratio compares sideways contraction to lengthwise stretch.
Elasticity covers Young's modulus, bulk modulus and rigidity modulus; Poisson's ratio is the simplest to use in direct questions.

terms.meaning: Restoring force per unit area, F/A.
Change in length divided by original length.
Change in diameter divided by original diameter.
Lateral strain/longitudinal strain; dimensionless.
Stress/longitudinal strain.

formulas: Stress = F/A; strain = delta L/L
Young's modulus Y = (F/A)/(delta L/L) = F*L/(A*delta L)
Bulk modulus B = -P/(delta V/V); compressibility = 1/B
Rigidity modulus G = shear stress/shear strain
Poisson's ratio sigma = lateral strain/longitudinal strain
Lateral strain = sigma*longitudinal strain
Theoretical limits: -1 to 0.5; usual materials 0.2 to 0.5
Elastic energy per volume = (1/2)*stress*strain
Y = 3*B*(1 - 2*sigma) = 2*G*(1 + sigma)
Work to stretch a wire = (1/2)*F*delta L
Spring constant of a wire: k = Y*A/L, so F = k*delta L
Elastic energy stored = (1/2)*Y*(strain)^2*volume
Thermal stress = Y*alpha*delta T (rod clamped at both ends)
Hooke's law: stress is proportional to strain within the elastic limit
Change in diameter: delta D/D = sigma*(delta L/L); volume change dV/V = (delta L/L)*(1 - 2*sigma)
how: Under a pull the wire extends by delta L over length L. Volume tends to be conserved, so the cross-section shrinks. The ratio of these two strains is a material constant for small loads (Hooke's law region).
With the numbers given: lateral strain = 0.5*0.02 = 0.01. Sign is opposite (a contraction), but questions use magnitudes.
cases: Maximum value 0.5 means volume stays constant (rubber is near 0.5)
Steel about 0.28, copper about 0.35
Strain has no unit and no dimension
Stress unit is Pa (N/m^2)
Beyond the elastic limit, permanent deformation remains
Same Y for a material regardless of wire size
Stress-strain curve order: proportional limit, elastic limit, yield point, ultimate strength, fracture
Ductile materials stretch a lot before breaking; brittle materials break with little strain
Wires with higher Young's modulus stretch less for the same load
values: Y for steel about 2*10^11 Pa; copper about 1.1*10^11 Pa
Poisson's ratio has no units
Bulk modulus of water about 2.2*10^9 Pa
uses: Wire extension under a load
Structural design with steel cables
Elastic limit and safety factor checks
mistakes: Multiplying by the length instead of using strain directly
Confusing lateral with longitudinal strain
Treating Poisson's ratio as having a unit
Taking sigma above 0.5
Forgetting the negative sign in the physical definition of Poisson's ratio when lateral strain is a contraction
exam: AAI style: one-step substitution.
Practice: longitudinal strain 0.04, sigma 0.25, lateral strain? (0.01)
wire L = 2 m extends 1 mm, strain? (0.0005)
Y with stress 2*10^8 Pa and strain 0.001? (2*10^11 Pa)
sigma of ideal incompressible solid? (0.5)

topics.title: Heat, Temperature and Temperature Scales
overview: Temperature tells how hot a body is (average molecular kinetic energy). Heat is energy that flows from a hot body to a cold body only because of a temperature difference. It is a process quantity, not something stored in a body.
This is the base of thermodynamics. AAI questions test the heat versus internal energy idea, calorimetry (mixing) and conversions between Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin scales.

terms.meaning: Energy in transit due to a temperature difference; SI unit joule (also calorie, 1 cal = 4.18 J).
Measure of average translational kinetic energy of molecules; decides the direction of heat flow.
Total kinetic plus potential energy of molecules; this IS a property a body possesses.
Heat needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1 K; Q = m*s*dT.
Heat per unit mass absorbed or released during a phase change at constant temperature; Q = m*L.
Measuring heat exchange using the principle: heat lost by hot body = heat gained by cold body.

formulas: C/5 = (F - 32)/9 (Celsius-Fahrenheit conversion).
K = C + 273.15 (Kelvin-Celsius); a change of 1 K equals a change of 1 C.
F = (9/5)*C + 32; a change of 9 F equals a change of 5 C.
Q = m*s*dT (heat for temperature change, no phase change).
Q = m*L (heat for phase change).
Calorimetry: m1*s1*(T1 - T) = m2*s2*(T - T2) for final mixture temperature T.
Heat capacity = m*s; water equivalent W = m*s/s_water (mass of water with the same heat capacity).
Same reading on both scales at -40 (C = F = -40).
Zeroth law: if A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in equilibrium with each other.
Kelvin-Fahrenheit: (K - 273.15)/5 = (F - 32)/9.
First law: Q = dU + W; heat is path dependent, internal energy U is a state function.
Thermal expansion: dL = L*alpha*dT; dV = V*gamma*dT with gamma = 3*alpha.
Mixture with phase change: heat given by hot body = m*s*dT + m*L of the cold body; first check whether all the ice melts.
how: Heat flows only while two bodies are at different temperatures. Once temperatures equalise (thermal equilibrium) there is no net flow.
Hence heat is energy being transferred; a single body at rest does not have a quantity called heat content, it has internal energy.

The Celsius and Fahrenheit scales are both linear. Water freezes at 0 C and 32 F, boils at 100 C and 212 F, so 100 C divisions match 180 F divisions. This gives the ratio 5:9, and the offset 32 gives C/5 = (F-32)/9.
In calorimetry energy is conserved: if no heat is lost to surroundings, heat lost by hot bodies equals heat gained by cold bodies, which gives the final temperature.
cases: Two bodies at the same temperature can differ in internal energy (different mass or material), but no heat flows between them.
Bodies of different masses at the same temperature: the larger one has more internal energy.
During melting or boiling temperature stays constant even though heat is supplied (latent heat).
Heat flows from high to low temperature, never the reverse by itself.
Heat gained is positive, heat lost is negative in sign convention; the sum is zero in an isolated mixture.
Absolute zero is 0 K = -273.15 C = -459.67 F.
values: Ice point: 0 C = 32 F = 273.15 K.
Steam point: 100 C = 212 F = 373.15 K.
Specific heat of water: 4200 J/(kg K) or 1 cal/(g C).
Latent heat of fusion of ice: 336 kJ/kg (80 cal/g); of vaporization of water: 2260 kJ/kg (540 cal/g).
Body temperature: 37 C = 98.6 F.
uses: Finding the final temperature when hot and cold liquids are mixed.
Weather and cockpit or ATC data given in different scales; airport temperature corrections.
Understanding why heat is called energy in transit in thermodynamic statements.
mistakes: Saying a body 'contains' heat; it contains internal energy, heat is only transferred.
Using C = (5/9)*F without subtracting 32 first.
Using 273 for Kelvin when the question needs an exact ratio, or adding 273 to a temperature difference.
Forgetting latent heat when a phase change occurs during mixing.
Treating heat capacity (J/K, for the whole body) and specific heat (J/kg K, per unit mass) as the same.
exam: AAI JE style: a direct 'which statement is incorrect/correct about heat' conceptual item or a one-step scale conversion.
Practice: 86 F in C? [30 C]. 50 C in F? [122 F]. At what temperature do C and F readings match? [-40]. Change of 18 F equals how many C? [10 C].

topics.title: Kinetic Theory: Degrees of Freedom and RMS Speed
overview: Kinetic theory explains gas properties (pressure, temperature) from random motion of molecules. Two key results are the RMS speed, which depends on temperature, and the equipartition of energy among degrees of freedom.
In the syllabus it connects the ideal gas law with molecular motion and leads to specific heats of gases. Questions are mostly short formula or concept checks.

terms.meaning: Number of independent ways a molecule can store energy: translation, rotation and vibration modes.
Square root of the mean of squares of molecular speeds, v_rms = sqrt(3RT/M).
Gas of point molecules with no intermolecular forces, obeying PV = nRT.
Each degree of freedom carries average energy (1/2)*k*T per molecule at temperature T.
A process at constant temperature, so PV = constant.
Mass of one mole of gas, in kg/mol in the speed formula.

formulas: v_rms = sqrt(3RT/M) = sqrt(3kT/m) = sqrt(3P/rho).
Average speed v_avg = sqrt(8RT/(pi*M)); most probable speed v_mp = sqrt(2RT/M).
v_rms : v_avg : v_mp = sqrt(3) : sqrt(8/pi) : sqrt(2) = 1.224 : 1.128 : 1.
Average KE per molecule = (3/2)*k*T; per mole = (3/2)*R*T.
Energy per degree of freedom per molecule = (1/2)*k*T.
Internal energy of n moles: U = (f/2)*n*R*T.
Pressure: P = (1/3)*rho*v_rms^2; PV = (1/3)*N*m*v_rms^2.
Isothermal: P1*V1 = P2*V2 at constant T.
Graham law: rate of diffusion is proportional to 1/sqrt(M) at same T and P.
Mean free path = 1/(sqrt(2)*pi*d^2*n), n = molecules per unit volume.
Dalton law: total pressure of a gas mixture = sum of partial pressures.
Mayer relation: Cp - Cv = R; at equal T, v_rms is proportional to sqrt(T) and the mean KE depends only on T.
how: From PV = (1/3)*N*m*v^2 and PV = N*k*T we get (1/2)*m*v_rms^2 = (3/2)*k*T. Hence v_rms depends only on T and the molecular mass, not on pressure or volume separately.
If pressure is changed at constant temperature, the volume changes inversely, but the molecules keep the same average kinetic energy, so v_rms is unchanged.
A point mass has 3 translational degrees of freedom. A rigid diatomic molecule (dumbbell) adds 2 rotations about the axes perpendicular to the bond.
Rotation about the bond axis is negligible because the atoms are point-like. So f = 5. At high temperature vibration adds 2 more (kinetic plus potential), giving 7.
cases: Monoatomic gas (He, Ne, Ar): f = 3, gamma = 5/3.
Diatomic rigid (O2, N2, H2 at room T): f = 5, gamma = 7/5 = 1.4.
Diatomic with vibration (very high T): f = 7, gamma = 9/7.
Nonlinear polyatomic (rigid): f = 6, gamma = 4/3; linear polyatomic like CO2 (rigid): f = 5.
Doubling temperature multiplies v_rms by sqrt(2); at same T lighter gases move faster.
v_rms is independent of pressure, volume (at fixed T) and of the amount of gas.
values: Cv for diatomic = (5/2)*R; Cp = (7/2)*R.
Avogadro number N_A = 6.02*10^23 per mol.
Ratio of v_rms for H2 and O2 at same T = sqrt(32/2) = 4.
uses: Comparing molecular speeds of different gases and temperatures (diffusion, escape of gases).
Finding specific heats and gamma used in adiabatic processes, sound speed in gases.
Reasoning on gas behaviour in aircraft cabin and tyre pressure changes.
mistakes: Thinking RMS speed changes with pressure in an isothermal process; only T matters.
Counting 6 degrees of freedom for diatomic gas (rotation about the molecular axis is excluded) or adding vibration at room temperature.
Using M in grams per mole instead of kg per mole in v_rms.
Mixing up v_rms, average and most probable speeds order: rms is the largest.
Forgetting that mean KE per molecule is the same for all ideal gases at the same T, though their speeds differ.
exam: AAI JE style: 'find f for a given molecule' or 'how does v_rms change when P, V or T changes'.
Practice: v_rms if T becomes 4 times? [doubles]. gamma for monoatomic gas? [5/3]. U of 2 mol diatomic at 300 K? [(5/2)*2*R*300 = 1500R J]. Ratio v_rms of O2 to H2 at same T? [1/4].

topics.title: Newton's Law of Cooling
overview: Newton's law states that a hot body loses heat to its surroundings at a rate proportional to the temperature difference between the body and the surroundings, when this difference is small.
It is a standard calorimetry and heat-transfer topic. Exam problems give two cooling intervals and ask for the time of a third interval, which is solved with the average-temperature form.

terms.meaning: Fall in temperature per unit time, -dT/dt.
Constant temperature of the environment, the final limit of cooling.
Constant depending on surface area, mass, specific heat and surface nature of the body.
Difference T - T0 between the body and surroundings; it decides the cooling rate.
Approximation where the mean of start and end temperature is used for the excess temperature.

formulas: Differential form: dT/dt = -k*(T - T0).
Exact solution: T - T0 = (T_i - T0)*e^(-k*t), so excess falls exponentially.
Average form: (T1 - T2)/t = k*((T1 + T2)/2 - T0).
Time to fall by equal drops in two stages: t1/t2 = (average excess in stage 2)/(average excess in stage 1) for equal drops.
Heat loss rate: dQ/dt = m*s*(-dT/dt) = h*A*(T - T0).
Exact log form: ln((T1 - T0)/(T2 - T0)) = k*t.
Valid for small excess (about 30 K) with forced convection or radiation near T0.
k = h*A/(m*s) so cooling constant rises with area and falls with mass and specific heat.
how: Heat lost per second is proportional to excess temperature, and heat lost equals m*s times fall in temperature. So fall rate is proportional to excess: dT/dt = -k*(T - T0). Integrating gives an exponential decay of the excess.

For exam use, the exact log is avoided. The temperature fall in a short interval is taken proportional to the mean excess over that interval. Use the first case to get k, then apply to the second case.
Example: 70 to 40 in 5 min with T0 = 10: average excess 45, so 30/5 = 6 = 45*k, k = 2/15. Then 50 to 20: average excess 35 - 10 = 25, so 30/t = (2/15)*25, t = 9 min.
cases: Lower excess temperature means slower cooling, so equal drops take longer as the body gets closer to T0.
If T0 is not given in a problem, it must be found or assumed from the data.
Heating of a body (T less than T0) follows the same law with sign reversed.
Cooling time is infinite to reach exactly T0 in the exact model.
Larger surface area or better conducting surface gives larger k and faster cooling.
Equal drop in lower temperature range always needs more time than in the higher range.
Exact log method on the same data gives 10 min (ln(60/30) = ln 2 = 5k, then ln(40/10) = 2 ln 2 means 10 min); the exam keys the average-temperature answer 9 min, so follow the form the question uses.
Newton law follows from Stefan law for small excess: radiated power change is about 4*sigma*T0^3*A*(T - T0).
values: Units of k: per second (s^-1) or per minute.
Typical limit of validity: excess up to about 30 K.
Time constant = 1/k; excess falls to 1/e in that time.
uses: Estimating cooling time of tea, engines, brakes or hot metals.
Forensic estimate of time since a body cooled.
Design of radiators and heat sinks.
mistakes: Using the final or initial temperature alone instead of the average for the excess.
Forgetting to subtract the surrounding temperature.
Assuming equal time for equal temperature drops in different ranges.
Using exact exponential with the average form together and mixing results.
exam: AAI JE style: two data points of cooling plus a third interval; find time or final temperature.
Practice: 80 to 60 in 10 min, T0 = 20: time from 60 to 40? [k = 20/(10*50) = 0.04; 20/t = 0.04*30, so t = 16.7 min]. Doubling the excess doubles the rate? [yes]. Rate of cooling at T = T0? [zero]

topics.title: Simple Harmonic Motion: Phase, Velocity, Period
overview: Simple harmonic motion (SHM) is periodic motion in which the restoring force or acceleration is proportional to displacement and directed to the mean position. A simple pendulum for small angles and a mass on a spring are standard examples.
Questions test the SHM equation, phase, maximum velocity and acceleration, and the time period of a pendulum or spring.

terms.meaning: Maximum displacement from the mean position.
omega = 2*pi/T = 2*pi*f, in rad/s.
The whole argument (omega*t + phi) of the sine or cosine; it fixes the state of motion.
Initial phase, the phase at t = 0.
Time for one complete oscillation.
Force F = -k*x pulling the body back toward equilibrium.

formulas: Displacement: x = A*sin(omega*t + phi).
Velocity: v = A*omega*cos(omega*t + phi); v = omega*sqrt(A^2 - x^2).
Maximum velocity v_max = A*omega (at mean position).
Acceleration: a = -omega^2*x; maximum a = A*omega^2 (at extremes).
Time period of spring: T = 2*pi*sqrt(m/k).
Simple pendulum: T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g).
Total energy E = (1/2)*k*A^2 = (1/2)*m*omega^2*A^2; KE = (1/2)*m*omega^2*(A^2 - x^2).
Percentage change: dT/T = (1/2)*(dL/L) for small changes in L.
Frequency f = 1/T = omega/(2*pi).
Spring combinations: series k_eff = k1*k2/(k1 + k2); parallel k_eff = k1 + k2.
Pendulum with change in g: dT/T = -(1/2)*dg/g. In a lift accelerating up with a, T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/(g + a)).
Phase relations: x = A*cos(omega*t + phi) equals sin with phi + pi/2; frequency of energy exchange (KE or PE) is 2*f.
Kinetic energy equals potential energy at x = A/sqrt(2).
how: If F = -k*x, then m*d2x/dt2 = -k*x, so d2x/dt2 = -omega^2*x with omega^2 = k/m. The solution is a sinusoid, which is the SHM equation.
Differentiating x = A*sin(omega*t) gives v = A*omega*cos(omega*t); cosine has maximum 1, so v_max = A*omega. For x = 2 sin(40t), v_max = 2*40 = 80 m/s.
For a pendulum, T is proportional to sqrt(L). Taking logs and differentiating: dT/T = (1/2)*dL/L. A 10% rise in length gives about 5% rise in period (exact: sqrt(1.1) = 1.0488, about 4.9%).
cases: At the mean position: speed maximum, acceleration zero, KE maximum, PE zero.
At extreme positions: speed zero, acceleration maximum, KE zero.
Velocity leads displacement by pi/2 rad; acceleration is opposite in phase to displacement.
Period of a pendulum is independent of mass and amplitude (small angle).
Pendulum on the Moon (smaller g) has a longer period; in a freely falling lift it does not oscillate (effective g = 0).
Spring period unchanged by g; springs in series or parallel change effective k.
values: Pendulum with L = 1 m: T about 2 s on Earth (seconds pendulum).
Phase of y = a sin(3*pi*n*t + alpha) is 3*pi*n*t + alpha; angular frequency is 3*pi*n.
Phase difference of 2*pi means the same state.
uses: Analysis of vibrations in aircraft structures, instruments, springs and suspensions.
Timekeeping with pendulums and oscillators.
Finding energy or speed at a given displacement.
mistakes: Calling only omega*t the phase; the phase includes the epoch alpha.
Taking v_max as A/omega instead of A*omega.
Believing 10% length change gives 10% period change; it gives about 5%.
Using degrees in the sine argument when omega*t is in radians.
Forgetting that a pendulum clock gains or loses time when g or L changes; period shorter means the clock runs fast.
exam: AAI JE style: read amplitude, omega and phase from a given equation, or find percent change in T.
Practice: y = 3 sin(5t): v_max? [15]. a_max? [75]. Length increased by 21%: T change? [10%]. Period of spring m = 1 kg, k = 100 N/m? [2*pi/10 = 0.63 s].

topics.title: Wave Speed, Wavelength, Ultrasonics and Echo
overview: A wave transports energy with speed v = f*lambda, where f is frequency and lambda is wavelength. Sound is a longitudinal wave in a medium; ultrasonic waves have frequency above 20 kHz and cannot be heard by humans.
Questions use the basic wave relation, and echo or SONAR depth finding where the sound travels to a surface and back.

terms.meaning: Distance between two successive points in the same phase, e.g. crest to crest.
Number of vibrations per second, in hertz (Hz).
Distance a wave pulse travels per second, set by the medium.
Sound with frequency greater than 20 kHz.
Sound Navigation and Ranging; uses echoes of ultrasonic pulses to find depth or objects.
Reflected sound heard after a delay; needs at least 0.1 s gap, i.e. distance of about 17 m in air.

formulas: v = f*lambda = lambda/T.
lambda = v/f; for a given medium lambda is inversely proportional to f.
Echo or SONAR: 2*d = v*t, so d = v*t/2.
Speed of sound in air: v = sqrt(gamma*R*T/M); v about 331 + 0.6*T_c m/s.
Speed in liquid: v = sqrt(B/rho) (B = bulk modulus); in solid: sqrt(Y/rho).
1 MHz = 10^6 Hz and 1 kHz = 10^3 Hz.
Frequency does not change when a wave moves from one medium to another; v and lambda change.
Wave number k = 2*pi/lambda, omega = 2*pi*f, v = omega/k.
Wave on a string: v = sqrt(T/mu), T tension, mu mass per unit length.
Doppler effect: f_obs = f*(v +- v_o)/(v -+ v_s); approach raises frequency, recession lowers it.
Beats: beat frequency = |f1 - f2|. Closed pipe fundamental f = v/(4L); open pipe f = v/(2L).
Intensity level: beta = 10*log10(I/I0) dB, I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2.
how: In one period T a wave moves forward by one wavelength, so v = lambda/T = f*lambda. Speed is fixed by the medium, so a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength.
For the longest ultrasonic wavelength in air, take the lowest ultrasonic frequency, 20 kHz, and v = 340 m/s: lambda = 340/20000 = 0.017 m = 17 mm.

In echo problems the pulse travels to the target and back, so the distance travelled is twice the depth. With f = 0.06 MHz = 60000 Hz, v = 1700 m/s and t = 0.80 s: d = 1700*0.8/2 = 680 m and lambda = 1700/60000 = 0.0283 m.
For the tuning fork: lambda = 330/220 = 1.5 m.
cases: Infrasonic: below 20 Hz; audible: 20 Hz to 20 kHz; ultrasonic: above 20 kHz.
Sound is faster in solids than liquids than gases.
Sound speed in air increases with temperature, independent of pressure for an ideal gas.
Wavelength shrinks when the wave enters a slower medium at the same frequency.
Short wavelength ultrasound gives good directionality and resolution.
Echo needs minimum distance to the reflector of about 17 m.
values: Speed of sound in air at 20 C: about 343 m/s (340 m/s often used).
Sea water: about 1500 m/s (problem uses 1700 m/s given).
Steel: about 5000 m/s; water about 1480 m/s.
Audible range: 20 Hz to 20 kHz.
Bat and dolphin hearing range goes beyond 20 kHz.
Using 343 m/s instead of 340 m/s gives 17.15 mm for 20 kHz, still about 17 mm.
uses: SONAR for sea depth and submarines; ultrasonography and flaw detection in metals.
Cleaning, and bat or dolphin navigation.
Radar-like ranging logic is similar for radio waves in aviation (distance = c*t/2).
mistakes: Forgetting the factor 2 in echo distance.
Not converting MHz or kHz to Hz before dividing.
Using the highest frequency for the longest wavelength; the longest wavelength belongs to the lowest frequency.
Believing frequency changes with the medium.
exam: AAI JE style: given v, f and t, find depth and wavelength, or lambda from f.
Practice: echo after 2 s in air (340 m/s): distance? [340 m]. f = 500 Hz, v = 340 m/s: lambda? [0.68 m]. 40 kHz in air: lambda? [8.5 mm]. Wavelength 0.5 m, v = 330: f? [660 Hz].

topics.title: Coulomb Force and Field Superposition
overview: Electrostatics starts with Coulomb's law, the force between two point charges. From it we define the electric field E = F/q0 of a source charge.
Any number of charges act independently, so forces and fields are simply added as vectors (superposition principle).

Most numerical problems in the chapter reduce to three steps: find each force or field magnitude with k*q/r^2, fix its direction (away from positive, toward negative), and add as vectors. Symmetry often makes the sum zero or very simple.

terms.meaning: Force between two point charges is proportional to q1*q2 and inversely proportional to the square of their separation, along the line joining them.
Force per unit positive test charge, E = F/q0, in N/C or V/m.
Net force or field is the vector sum of the contributions from each charge separately.
Any charge is an integer multiple of e: Q = n*e.
Total charge of an isolated system stays constant.
A very small charge used to probe a field without disturbing the source.

formulas: F = k*q1*q2/r^2 with k = 1/(4*pi*eps0) = 9 * 10^9 N m^2/C^2, in vacuum or air.
In a medium of dielectric constant K: F = k*q1*q2/(K*r^2).
Point charge field: E = k*q/r^2, directed away from +q and toward -q.
Vector form: F on 2 due to 1 = k*q1*q2*r_hat/r^2, where r_hat points from 1 to 2.
Net field: E_net = E_1 + E_2 + ... (vector sum); two perpendicular parts give E = sqrt(E_1^2 + E_2^2).
Two fields at angle theta: E = sqrt(E_1^2 + E_2^2 + 2*E_1*E_2*cos(theta)).
Quantisation: Q = n*e, so n = Q/e, with e = 1.6 * 10^-19 C.
Circular orbit under Coulomb attraction: k*q1*q2/r^2 = m*v^2/r = m*omega^2*r, so T^2 = 16*pi^3*eps0*m*r^3/(q1*q2).
Equilibrium of a charge: sum of forces on it equals zero; compare magnitudes k*q/r^2 and fix the sign by direction.
Three equal charges q at corners of an equilateral triangle: field and force at the centroid is zero.
Field on the axis of a uniform ring (charge Q, radius R) at distance x from the centre: E = k*Q*x/(x^2 + R^2)^(3/2); zero at the centre, along the axis.
Field lines start on positive charges and end on negative charges, never cross, and are denser where the field is stronger.
how: Coulomb's law is an experimental inverse-square law, like Newton's gravitation but with both attraction and repulsion. Define the field as force per unit charge and the field of a source becomes independent of the test charge.
Since forces from different charges do not interfere, the total is a plain vector sum.
For orbit problems the Coulomb force plays the role of centripetal force. Putting omega = 2*pi/T gives T^2 proportional to r^3, the electrostatic version of Kepler's third law.
For equilibrium problems the distance ratio enters squared: a charge three times farther needs nine times the magnitude to balance.
Symmetry shortcut: n equal forces of equal size spread evenly around a point (angles 360/n degrees) cancel completely, so the net force at the centre of a regular polygon of equal charges is zero.
cases: Like charges repel, unlike charges attract; the force pair obeys Newton's third law.
Equal and opposite forces on Q from two charges on the same side of Q need opposite-sign charges; on opposite sides they need same-sign charges.
Doubling the separation reduces force to one-fourth; doubling a charge doubles the force.
Field direction: draw E_A and E_B at the field point using sign of each source, then resolve into x and y parts.
Right-triangle geometry (3-4-5 or 12-16-20) makes the two perpendicular field components easy to compute.
Neutral body: n electrons gained gives charge -n*e; electrons lost gives +n*e.
Charge on a conductor or in a closed system cannot be created or destroyed; rubbing only transfers electrons, so the two bodies get equal and opposite charge.
Force between two small identical conducting spheres after touching: the total charge is shared equally, so each has (q1 + q2)/2.
values: Mass of electron 9.1 * 10^-31 kg.
uses: Finding the net force or field due to several charges at a point.
Orbit of an electron around a nucleus in the Bohr-type model.
Counting excess or missing electrons from a given charge.
mistakes: Using r in cm instead of metres, which gives errors of 10^4 in k*q/r^2.
Adding magnitudes of fields without checking direction (vector sum needed).
Using ratio 3 instead of 3^2 = 9 when balancing forces at different distances.
Forgetting the sign: a negative charge's field points toward it.
Dropping the q1*q2 product in the orbit period formula (writing only q1).
Treating Coulomb's law as valid for extended bodies at short range; it is for point charges (or spheres, taking the centres).
exam: AAI style: a direct numerical Coulomb or superposition problem, or a symmetry argument giving zero force. Practice: (1) Force between 2 microC and 3 microC at 0.3 m? [0.6 N] (2) Field of 1 nC at 3 cm? [10^4 N/C]
(3) How many electrons make -3.2 microC? [2 * 10^13] (4) Force on charge at centroid of 4 equal charges at square corners? [zero]

topics.title: Electric Potential, Potential Energy and Zero-Potential Locus
overview: Electric potential V at a point is the work done per unit positive charge in bringing it from infinity to that point. Unlike the field it is a scalar, so potentials of several charges are added as plain numbers with signs.
Potential energy of a system of charges is the work needed to assemble it. Together these give quick ways to find where the potential vanishes and how much energy a configuration stores.

terms.meaning: Work per unit charge to bring a test charge from infinity to the point, V = W/q0, in volts.
Work done by an external agent to assemble the charges from infinite separation; U = q*V.
A surface on which V is the same everywhere; field is perpendicular to it.
V_B - V_A = work per unit charge to move from A to B.
Locus of points whose distances to two fixed points are in a constant ratio not equal to 1.

formulas: Point charge: V = k*q/r (scalar, sign follows q).
Many charges: V = k*q1/r1 + k*q2/r2 + ... (algebraic sum).
Two-charge energy: U = k*q1*q2/r12, relative to infinity.
Several charges: U = sum over pairs of k*qi*qj/rij.
Relation to field: E = -dV/dr; work W = q*(V_B - V_A).
Zero potential for q1 and q2: q1/r1 + q2/r2 = 0, so r2/r1 = -q2/q1 = |q2|/|q1| for opposite signs.
Dipole: V = k*p*cos(theta)/r^2 (zero on the equatorial line).
Kinetic energy gained by charge q through potential difference V: (1/2)*m*v^2 = q*V.
Conducting or hollow charged sphere of radius R: V = k*Q/r outside, V = k*Q/R on the surface and everywhere inside (constant), although E = 0 inside.
Field from potential: E = -dV/dx; E points from high to low potential, in the direction of steepest fall of V.
Work in an electric field is path independent: W = q*(V_A - V_B), and the work around any closed path is zero.
how: Potential is work per unit charge, and since the electric force is conservative, the work depends only on end points. For a point charge integrating E = k*q/r^2 from infinity to r gives V = k*q/r.
The potential of a group is the sum because work contributions add.
For the zero-potential locus of q and -2q, setting k*q/r1 - 2*k*q/r2 = 0 gives r2 = 2*r1. The locus is a circle because the ratio of distances is fixed at 2, not 1.
Finding its two points on the line joining the charges (one between, one outside the smaller charge) gives the diameter, hence centre and radius.
For potential energy, bringing the second charge in from infinity in the potential of the first costs q2 * (k*q1/r), which is the formula U = k*q1*q2/r.
cases: Like charges: U positive (repulsion, energy stored). Unlike charges: U negative (bound system).
Equal and opposite charges: zero-potential locus is the perpendicular bisector plane (a straight line in 2D).
Unequal opposite charges: locus is a circle that surrounds the smaller charge.
Moving along an equipotential needs no work; field lines cross equipotentials at right angles.
Potential at the midpoint of equal like charges is nonzero but field is zero; for equal unlike charges the reverse.
Potential is zero at infinity by convention.
A positive charge released from rest moves toward lower potential; a negative charge moves toward higher potential.
Potential inside a conductor in equilibrium is the same everywhere (the conductor is an equipotential).
values: Potential of 1 V = 1 J/C; 1 eV = 1.6 * 10^-19 J.
For q and -2q, 6 m apart: circle radius 4 m, centre 2 m beyond the smaller charge on the far side from the larger one (at -2 when q is at 0).
uses: Energy stored in charge clusters such as nuclei and molecules.
Accelerating charged particles through a voltage (electron guns, X-ray tubes).
Finding points where a combined potential vanishes.
mistakes: Using vector addition for potential; it is a scalar, signs only.
Forgetting the sign of charges when computing U for unlike charges.
Assuming the zero-potential locus is a straight line when charges have unequal magnitudes.
Mixing microC with C: 3 microC * 8 microC gives 24 * 10^-12 C^2.
Treating zero potential and zero field as the same thing.
Writing the potential energy of three charges as one pair only; all three pairs must be added.
exam: AAI style: a numerical U = k*q1*q2/r or a locus of V = 0 with two unequal charges. Practice: (1) U of 2 microC and 4 microC at 0.2 m? [0.36 J] (2) U for +2 microC and -2 microC at 0.1 m? [-0.36 J] (3) Potential 3 m from 1 nC? [3 V]
(4) Equal opposite charges: locus of V = 0? [perpendicular bisector]

topics.title: Electric Dipole: Field and Torque
overview: An electric dipole is a pair of equal and opposite charges +q and -q separated by a small distance 2a. Its strength is the dipole moment p = q * 2a, a vector pointing from -q to +q. Molecules such as water behave as dipoles.
The dipole field falls off as 1/r^3, faster than a single charge. In an external field the dipole feels zero net force (uniform field) but a torque that rotates it toward alignment with the field.

terms.meaning: Vector p = q * 2a, direction from negative to positive charge; unit C m.
One with separation much smaller than the distance r at which the field is measured.
The line through both charges; points on it are called end-on points.
The perpendicular bisector of the dipole.
Turning effect tau = p x E, a vector perpendicular to both p and E.

formulas: Axial field of short dipole: E = (1/4*pi*eps0)*(2p/r^3), along p direction.
Equatorial field: E = (1/4*pi*eps0)*(p/r^3), opposite to p.
General point: E = (k*p/r^3)*sqrt(1 + 3*cos^2(theta)), where theta is measured from p.
Axial field is twice the equatorial field at the same distance.
Torque: tau = p x E, magnitude p*E*sin(theta).
Potential energy in a field: U = -p.E = -p*E*cos(theta).
Net force in uniform field is zero; in a non-uniform field it is nonzero.
Work to rotate from theta1 to theta2: W = p*E*(cos(theta1) - cos(theta2)).
Potential of dipole: V = k*p*cos(theta)/r^2; V = 0 on the equatorial line.
Dipole in a non-uniform field: net force F = (p.grad)E, which is nonzero; torque still tends to align p with E.
how: On the axis, the fields of +q and -q point in opposite directions, and the nearer charge dominates. With distances r - a and r + a, E = k*q*(1/(r-a)^2 - 1/(r+a)^2) = 4*k*q*a*r/(r^2 - a^2)^2.

For r much greater than a this becomes 4*k*q*a/r^3 = 2*k*p/r^3. On the equatorial line the two fields have equal size; their components along the axis add and the perpendicular parts cancel, giving k*p/r^3 opposite to p.
In a uniform field the two forces +qE and -qE are equal and opposite, so there is no net force, yet they act at different points and create a couple. Its moment is q*E*2a*sin(theta) = p*E*sin(theta).
In vector form tau = p x E, hence by the rule of the cross product it is perpendicular to both p and E.
cases: Torque is maximum (p*E) when p is perpendicular to E; zero when p is parallel or antiparallel to E.
theta = 0 is stable equilibrium (U minimum, -p*E); theta = 180 degrees is unstable (U = +p*E).
The torque acts to align p with E, rotating the dipole in the plane containing both.
In a non-uniform field there is also a net force that pulls the dipole toward stronger field.
Direction of axial field is along p; direction of equatorial field is opposite to p.
Dielectric molecules are polar (permanent dipoles) or non-polar (induced dipoles).
values: Unit of p: C m (also debye; 1 D = 3.3 * 10^-30 C m).
Axial : equatorial field ratio = 2 : 1 at equal distance.
uses: Behaviour of polar molecules (water, HCl) in electric fields and microwaves.
Understanding polarisation in dielectrics.
Atomic and molecular models of charge distribution.
mistakes: Using p/r^3 instead of 2p/r^3 on the axis (or vice versa on the equator).
Saying the torque is parallel to p or E; it is perpendicular to both.
Forgetting that net force on a dipole in a uniform field is zero.
Confusing dipole moment direction: it points from negative to positive charge.
Using the dipole formulas for points close to the dipole (r comparable to 2a).
exam: AAI style: a conceptual statement about the direction of torque or the formula of axial field. Practice: (1) Axial field of p = 10^-9 C m at 0.1 m? [1.8 * 10^4 N/C] (2) Max torque for p = 2 * 10^-9 C m in 10^3 N/C? [2 * 10^-6 N m]
(3) Equilibrium at which angle is stable? [0 degrees] (4) Dipole potential on equatorial line? [zero]

topics.title: Gauss Law and Electric Flux
overview: Electric flux measures how much field passes through a surface. Gauss's law states that the total flux through any closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by eps0. It is the easiest way to find fields for symmetrical charge distributions.
The same ideas give fields of infinite wire, plane sheet and sphere, the flux of a point charge through a face or a cap, and the jump in field across a charged plate.

terms.meaning: phi = E.A = E*A*cos(theta), where A is the area vector along the normal.
Net flux through a closed surface = Q_enclosed/eps0.
An imaginary closed surface chosen to match the symmetry of the problem.
lambda = charge per unit length, C/m.
sigma = charge per unit area, C/m^2.
Measure of the cone subtended at a point; total solid angle is 4*pi.

formulas: Flux: phi = E.A = E*A*cos(theta); theta is the angle between E and the normal.
Gauss: integral of E.dA over a closed surface = Q_enclosed/eps0.
Infinite line charge: E = lambda/(2*pi*eps0*r), radially outward for lambda positive.
Infinite sheet: E = sigma/(2*eps0), independent of distance; near a conductor E = sigma/eps0.
Uniformly charged sphere or shell outside: E = k*Q/r^2; inside a shell: E = 0.
Cube with charge q at centre: flux through each face = q/(6*eps0).
Flux through a disk on the axis of a point charge: phi = (Q/(2*eps0))*(1 - cos(theta)), with tan(theta) = R/h.
